See? It's just sine and cosine. The math is simple. The IDEA of encoding position as multi-frequency oscillations is what's brilliant.
The Feed-Forward Network: The "Think" Step
After self-attention, each token's representation is passed through a Feed-Forward Network (FFN). This is a simple two-layer neural network applied independently to each token:
In the original Transformer:
Input dimension: d_model = 512
Hidden dimension: d_ff = 2048 (4× the model dimension)
Activation: ReLU (max(0, x))
The FFN expands the 512-dimensional representation to 2048 dimensions, applies ReLU, and then projects it back to 512 dimensions.

Why is this necessary? Self-attention is a linear operation (weighted sum). It can mix information between tokens, but it can't perform non-linear transformations. The FFN adds non-linearity, allowing the model to learn complex, non-linear relationships.

Analogy 1: The Think Step. Self-attention is like a group discussion. Everyone shares information. But after the discussion, each person needs to go to their office and think about what they heard. The FFN is the "think" step. Each token takes the information gathered from self-attention and processes it independently, extracting higher-level features.

Analogy 2: The Kitchen. Self-attention is like gathering ingredients from different parts of the kitchen. The FFN is like cooking: you take the gathered ingredients, apply heat (ReLU), and transform them into something new. The output is a dish that is more than the sum of its ingredients.

📝 TL;DR: The FFN is a two-layer neural network (512 → 2048 → 512) applied independently to each token. It adds non-linearity to the model, allowing it to learn complex relationships. Self-attention gathers information; the FFN processes it.
Embeddings and Softmax
The Transformer has two mapping layers:

Input Embedding: The input tokens (e.g., words or subwords) are mapped to dense vectors of dimension d_model = 512. This is a learned lookup table. Each token in the vocabulary has a 512-dimensional embedding vector.
The embeddings are multiplied by √d_model before adding the positional encoding. This scaling ensures that the embedding magnitudes are comparable to the positional encoding magnitudes.

Output Softmax: The decoder's output is a 512-dimensional vector for each position. This is projected to the vocabulary size (e.g., 37,000 for BPE) using a linear layer, and then softmax is applied to get a probability distribution over the vocabulary.
The token with the highest probability is selected as the output (during inference). During training, the cross-entropy loss is computed between the predicted distribution and the true target token.
Analogy: The Translator's Dictionary.
The input embedding is like looking up a word in a dictionary. You find the word "cat" and get its definition (a 512-dimensional vector that encodes its meaning).
The output softmax is like choosing the right word from a list of 37,000 candidates. The model assigns a probability to each candidate, and the one with the highest probability wins.

📝 TL;DR: The input embedding maps tokens to 512-dimensional vectors (scaled by √d_model). The output softmax maps the decoder's 512-dimensional output to a probability distribution over the vocabulary. The highest-probability token is selected as the output.
Why Self-Attention Beats RNNs and CNNs
The Transformer paper includes a comparison table that shows why self-attention is superior to recurrence and convolution for sequence modeling:
Where n is the sequence length, d is the representation dimension, and k is the kernel size.
Key insights:

Self-Attention has O(1) maximum path length. Any two tokens can communicate in a single step. In an RNN, tokens 1 and 50 are 49 steps apart. In a CNN with kernel size 3, they are log_3(50) ≈ 4 steps apart. In self-attention, they are 1 step apart.

Self-Attention has O(1) sequential operations. All attention computations happen in parallel. An RNN has O(n) sequential operations (one per token). This is why Transformers train so much faster on GPUs.

Self-Attention has O(n²) complexity per layer. This is the downside. For very long sequences (n > 10,000), the n² term becomes prohibitive. This is the problem that FlashAttention and sparse attention address (Chapter 14).
Analogy: The Communication Network.
RNN is like a telephone game. Messages are passed one person at a time. The path from person 1 to person 50 is 49 hops.
CNN is like a hierarchical organization. Person 1 talks to their manager, who talks to their director, who talks to the CEO. The path is log(n) hops.
Self-Attention is like a roundtable. Every person can talk to every other person directly. The path is 1 hop.

📝 TL;DR: Self-attention has O(1) maximum path length (any two tokens can communicate in one step) and O(1) sequential operations (fully parallelizable). This makes it faster and better at capturing long-range dependencies than RNNs and CNNs. The trade-off is O(n²) complexity per layer, which becomes expensive for very long sequences.
Training: Data, BPE, Batching
The Transformer was trained on two translation datasets:
WMT 2014 English-German: 4.5 million sentence pairs.
WMT 2014 English-French: 36 million sentence pairs.

Tokenization: Byte Pair Encoding (BPE). The Transformer doesn't operate on whole words. It uses Byte Pair Encoding (BPE), a subword tokenization method. BPE starts with individual characters and iteratively merges the most frequent pairs. For example:
"lowest" → "low" + "est"
"unhappiness" → "un" + "happiness"
This gives a vocabulary of about 37,000 tokens for English-German and 32,000 for English-French. BPE handles rare words and morphological variations gracefully.

Batching: Training examples are batched together. Each batch contains approximately 25,000 source tokens and 25,000 target tokens. Sequences of similar length are grouped together to minimize padding.

Analogy: The Subword Lego. BPE is like breaking words into Lego bricks. "Unhappiness" is not a single, solid piece. It's built from "un," "happi," and "ness." If the model has seen "un" and "ness" before, it can understand "unhappiness" even if it has never seen the whole word.

📝 TL;DR: The Transformer was trained on 4.5M En-De and 36M En-Fr sentence pairs. It uses BPE tokenization (37K vocabulary) to handle rare words and morphology. Batches contain ~25K tokens, grouped by length to minimize padding.
Training: The Adam Optimizer and Warmup Schedule
The Transformer uses the Adam optimizer (which we explored in Chapter 7) with a custom learning rate schedule:
lr = d_model^(-0.5) × min(step^(-0.5), step × warmup_steps^(-1.5))
Where warmup_steps = 4000.
This schedule has two phases:

Warmup (steps 1-4000): The learning rate increases linearly from 0 to its maximum. This prevents the model from diverging in the early stages of training, when the weights are random and the gradients are noisy.
Decay (steps 4001+): The learning rate decreases proportionally to the inverse square root of the step number. This allows the model to converge to a good solution.
Analogy: The Car Acceleration.
Warmup is like gently pressing the gas pedal when starting a car. You don't floor it from 0 to 100 mph instantly. You accelerate gradually to avoid losing control.
Decay is like easing off the gas pedal as you approach your destination. You slow down to park smoothly, instead of slamming into the curb.

📝 TL;DR: The Transformer uses Adam with a warmup schedule: the learning rate increases linearly for the first 4,000 steps, then decreases with the inverse square root of the step number. This prevents early divergence and enables smooth convergence.
Training: Dropout and Label Smoothing

Dropout (rate = 0.1): Dropout is applied to the output of each sub-layer (before the residual connection) and to the embeddings. During training, 10% of the activations are randomly set to zero. This prevents overfitting.
Label Smoothing (ε = 0.1): Instead of training with hard labels (e.g., "the correct word is 'cat' with probability 1.0"), label smoothing uses soft labels:
Correct word: probability = 1 - ε = 0.9
All other words: probability = ε / (V - 1) ≈ 0.000003 (spread uniformly)
This prevents the model from becoming overconfident. It encourages the model to assign some probability to alternative translations, which improves generalization.
Analogy: The Strict vs. Lenient Teacher.
Hard labels are like a strict teacher who only accepts the exact right answer. "The answer is 42. Anything else is wrong."

Label smoothing is like a lenient teacher who says, "The answer is probably 42, but 41 and 43 are also reasonable. Let's give them some credit." This prevents the student from memorizing exact answers and encourages them to understand the underlying concept.

📝 TL;DR: The Transformer uses dropout (10%) to prevent overfitting and label smoothing (ε=0.1) to prevent overconfidence. Label smoothing assigns 90% probability to the correct word and spreads 10% across all other words.
Results: BLEU Scores and What They Mean
The Transformer achieved state-of-the-art results on both translation tasks:

What is BLEU? BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy) is a metric that measures how similar the machine translation is to human reference translations. It ranges from 0 to 100. Higher is better. A BLEU score of 28.4 means the translation is quite good, though not perfect (human translators typically score 50-60+ against each other).
Key takeaways:
The Transformer (big) outperformed all previous models on both tasks.
The Transformer (base) achieved competitive results with a fraction of the training cost.
Training time was dramatically reduced: 12 hours for the base model vs. weeks for comparable RNN models.

This means the model went from being a theoretical curiosity to the new state-of-the-art, while training 10-100x faster than RNN-based models. In practical terms, it made high-quality neural machine translation accessible to researchers without massive compute budgets.

📝 TL;DR: The Transformer achieved 28.4 BLEU on En-De and 41.8 BLEU on En-Fr, outperforming all previous models. The base model trained in 12 hours on 8 GPUs, compared to weeks for RNN-based models. The combination of better quality and faster training was unprecedented.
Ablation Studies: What Happens When You Remove Things
The paper includes extensive ablation studies, where individual components are modified or removed to measure their impact. Here are the key findings:
Key insights:
Multi-head attention matters. Reducing from 8 heads to 1 head drops BLEU by 1.5 points. Multiple heads capture different types of relationships.
Key dimension matters. Reducing d_k from 64 to 16 drops BLEU by 1.3 points. The attention computation needs enough capacity.
Dropout and label smoothing matter. Removing either one drops BLEU by 0.5-0.7 points. Regularization is important.
Positional encoding type doesn't matter much. Learned and sinusoidal positional encodings perform similarly.

Analogy: The Car Tuning. Ablation studies are like tuning a car. You change one component at a time (swap the tires, change the oil, adjust the suspension) and measure the effect on performance. This tells you which components matter and which don't.

📝 TL;DR: Ablation studies show that multi-head attention (8 heads), sufficient key dimension (d_k=64), dropout, and label smoothing are all important. Positional encoding type (learned vs. sinusoidal) doesn't matter much.
English Constituency Parsing: Proving Generality
To prove that the Transformer is not just a translation model, the authors applied it to English constituency parsing: the task of breaking a sentence into a hierarchical tree structure.
For example, the sentence "The cat sat on the mat" would be parsed as:
(S (NP (DT The) (NN cat)) (VP (VBD sat) (PP (IN on) (NP (DT the) (NN mat)))))

The Transformer achieved a state-of-the-art F1 score of 92.7 on the WSJ Penn Treebank, outperforming specialized parsing models. This demonstrated that the Transformer is a general-purpose sequence model, not just a translation architecture.

Why does this matter? It showed that the Transformer's self-attention mechanism is powerful enough to learn hierarchical structure, even though the architecture has no explicit notion of hierarchy. The attention heads learn to capture syntactic relationships (subject-verb, noun-adjective) without being told what they are.

📝 TL;DR: The Transformer achieved state-of-the-art results on English constituency parsing (F1 = 92.7), proving that it's a general-purpose sequence model, not just a translation architecture. Self-attention can learn hierarchical structure without explicit supervision.
The Legacy: How This Paper Led to Everything

The Transformer paper is the most cited paper in AI history, with over 130,000 citations. But citations don't capture its true impact. The Transformer is the architectural foundation of virtually every modern AI system.
Here is the family tree:
2017: Transformer (Vaswani et al.)
Encoder-decoder architecture for translation.
2018: GPT-1 (Radford et al.)
Transformer decoder only. Trained on text generation (predict the next token).
Proved that a Transformer decoder can learn language from unlabeled text.
2018: BERT (Devlin et al.)
Transformer encoder only. Trained on masked language modeling (predict the masked token).
Proved that a Transformer encoder can learn bidirectional context.
2019: GPT-2 (Radford et al.)
Larger Transformer decoder. 1.5B parameters. Showed emergent zero-shot abilities.
2020: GPT-3 (Brown et al.)
175B parameter Transformer decoder. Few-shot learning. In-context learning.
2020: ViT (Dosovitskiy et al.)
Transformer applied to images. Cut images into patches, treat them as tokens.
2021: DALL-E (Ramesh et al.)
Transformer for text-to-image generation.
2022: ChatGPT (OpenAI)
GPT-3.5 with RLHF. Transformer decoder + human feedback.
2023: GPT-4 (OpenAI)
Multimodal Transformer. Text + images.
2023: LLaMA (Meta)
Open-source Transformer decoder. Democratized LLMs.
2024-2026: GPT-5, Gemini 2.5, Claude 4, Qwen 3.8, DeepSeek-V3, LLaMA 4
All Transformers. All descendants of Vaswani et al. (2017).

Every chatbot you've talked to. Every image generator you've used. Every code assistant. Every translation service. Every AI system. They are all Transformers. They are all descendants of this single paper.
Eight people. One paper. A revolution.

📝 TL;DR: The Transformer is the architectural foundation of modern AI. GPT is a Transformer decoder. BERT is a Transformer encoder. ViT is a Transformer for images. DALL-E is a Transformer for generation. ChatGPT is a Transformer with RLHF. Every modern AI system is a descendant of Vaswani et al. (2017).
Explain It to a 10-Year-Old
Imagine you are in a classroom with 30 students. The teacher asks a question, and everyone needs to work together to find the answer.

In the old way (RNN), the teacher whispers the question to student 1, who whispers it to student 2, who whispers it to student 3, and so on. By the time it reaches student 30, the question is garbled. And it takes forever, because each student has to wait for the previous one.

In the new way (Transformer), the teacher writes the question on the board. All 30 students can see it at the same time. Each student looks at every other student's answer and decides which ones are most helpful. They all work together, simultaneously, in one step.

The Transformer is the new way. Every word in a sentence can talk to every other word at the same time. No whispering. No waiting. No garbled messages. Everyone hears everyone. And because they all work at the same time, it's incredibly fast.
That's why the paper is called "Attention Is All You Need." You don't need the telephone game. You just need everyone to pay attention to everyone else.
💡 WHY SHOULD YOU CARE?

The Transformer is the most important invention in the history of artificial intelligence. It is the architecture behind every AI system you have ever used. ChatGPT is a Transformer. Google Translate is a Transformer. DALL-E is a Transformer. Siri is a Transformer. The AI that writes your emails, generates your images, translates your documents, and answers your questions is a Transformer.

Understanding the Transformer is not optional. It is the key to understanding modern AI. And now, after walking through every component, every equation, and every numerical example, you understand it.
You are no longer a spectator. You are literate.
🔗 WHAT IT LED TO

Transformer (2017) → GPT-1 (2018) → BERT (2018) → GPT-2 (2019) → GPT-3 (2020) → ViT (2020) → DALL-E (2021) → ChatGPT (2022) → GPT-4 (2023) → LLaMA (2023) → Gemini (2023) → Claude (2023) → Qwen (2023) → DeepSeek (2024) → GPT-5 (2025) → Every modern AI system.
⚠️ LIMITATIONS AND CRITICISMS

O(n²) Complexity: Self-attention requires every token to attend to every other token. For a sequence of length n, this is n² operations. For n=100,000 (a long document), this is 10 billion operations. This is the bottleneck that FlashAttention and sparse attention address (Chapter 14).
Memory Intensive: The attention matrix is n × n. For n=10,000, this is a 100-million-element matrix. Storing this in GPU memory is expensive.

No Built-in Hierarchy: The Transformer treats all tokens equally. It has no explicit notion of hierarchical structure (e.g., words form phrases, phrases form sentences). It must learn hierarchy implicitly through attention patterns.

Positional Encoding Limitations: The original sinusoidal positional encoding may not generalize well to very long sequences. Modern models use rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) or other alternatives.
Training Instability: Very deep Transformers can be unstable to train. Pre-LN (LayerNorm before the sub-layer) and careful initialization are needed for stability.
CHAPTER SUMMARY AND CONNECTIONS
In this chapter, we explored the most important paper in AI history: "Attention Is All You Need" by Vaswani et al. (2017).

We saw how the Transformer throws away recurrence entirely and builds the entire architecture from self-attention, feed-forward networks, residual connections, and layer normalization. We walked through the encoder stack (6 layers of self-attention + FFN) and the decoder stack (6 layers of masked self-attention + cross-attention + FFN).

We computed attention for "The cat sat" with actual numbers, from embedding to Q/K/V to softmax to weighted sum. We saw how multi-head attention splits the computation into 8 parallel heads, each learning a different type of relationship. We computed positional encodings with sine and cosine functions.
We explored the training details: BPE tokenization, Adam with warmup, dropout, label smoothing. We saw the results: 28.4 BLEU on En-De, 41.8 BLEU on En-Fr, trained in hours instead of weeks.
And we traced the legacy: from GPT to BERT to ViT to ChatGPT to GPT-5. Every modern AI system is a descendant of this paper.
The Transformer is not just an architecture. It is the foundation of the AI revolution. And now, you understand it completely.

In the next chapter, Chapter 14: Making Attention Faster — FlashAttention & Friends, we will tackle the Transformer's biggest limitation: the O(n²) complexity of self-attention. We will see how FlashAttention makes attention 2-4x faster without approximation, how sparse attention reduces the number of tokens each token attends to, and how linear attention approximates the attention matrix with kernel methods.
The Transformer conquered AI. Now, let's make it faster.

chapters.title: Making Attention Faster — FlashAttention & Friends

blocks.text: SECTION 1: CHAPTER OPENING HOOK
The Transformer conquered AI. There is no other way to say it.

From language to vision, from audio to protein folding, from chatbots to image generators, the Transformer is the foundation of everything. It is the most important architecture in the history of artificial intelligence.
But the Transformer has a fatal flaw. A mathematical Achilles' heel that threatens to limit everything it can do.
The flaw is three characters long: O(n²).

Self-attention requires every token to attend to every other token. For a sequence of n tokens, that's n × n attention scores. For n = 1,000 (a short paragraph), that's 1,000,000 operations. Manageable. For n = 10,000 (a long document), that's 100,000,000 operations. Getting expensive. For n = 100,000 (a book), that's 10,000,000,000 operations. Prohibitive.

And it's not just compute. The attention matrix itself is n × n. For n = 10,000, that's a 100-million-element matrix. Storing it in GPU memory requires gigabytes of fast memory. For n = 100,000, it requires terabytes. No GPU on Earth has that much memory.

This is the O(n²) wall. And it means that the Transformer, the architecture that conquered AI, cannot natively process a book, a long video, a genome, or a full day of audio. It runs out of memory. It runs out of time. It hits the wall.

This chapter is the story of the race to break through that wall. We will explore FlashAttention, which makes exact attention 2-4x faster by reorganizing the computation. We will explore Longformer and Big Bird, which use sparse attention to reduce the number of connections. We will explore Linformer and Performers, which approximate the attention matrix with linear complexity. And we will explore the survey that cataloged them all.
The Transformer conquered AI. Now, let's make it faster.
SECTION 2: THE PROBLEM
To understand why O(n²) is such a problem, let's walk through the attention computation step by step.
For a sequence of n tokens, each with embedding dimension d:
Step 1: Compute Q, K, V. Three matrix multiplications: X × W_Q, X × W_K, X × W_V.
Complexity: O(n × d²). This is linear in n. Fine.
Step 2: Compute Attention Scores. Multiply Q by K^T: Q × K^T.
Q is n × d. K^T is d × n. The result is n × n.
Complexity: O(n² × d). This is quadratic in n.
Step 3: Apply Softmax. Apply softmax to each row of the n × n matrix.
Complexity: O(n²). Quadratic in n.
Step 4: Multiply by V. Multiply the attention weights (n × n) by V (n × d).
Complexity: O(n² × d). Quadratic in n.
The bottleneck is Steps 2, 3, and 4. They all scale with n². Double the sequence length, and the computation quadruples. Triple it, and the computation increases ninefold.

But there's an even worse problem: memory. The n × n attention matrix must be stored in GPU memory. For n = 10,000 and float16 precision, the matrix is 10,000 × 10,000 × 2 bytes = 200 MB. For n = 100,000, it's 20 GB. For n = 1,000,000, it's 2 TB. No GPU has that much memory.

This is why, for years, the maximum context length of Transformer models was stuck at 512 or 1,024 tokens. BERT used 512. GPT-2 used 1,024. GPT-3 pushed it to 2,048. But beyond that, the O(n²) wall was insurmountable.
The field needed a breakthrough. And it came from two directions:
Make exact attention faster (FlashAttention): Don't change the math. Change how the math is executed on the GPU.
Approximate attention (Sparse, Linear, Kernel): Change the math to reduce the complexity from O(n²) to O(n log n) or O(n).
Let's explore both.
SECTION: PAPER 1: FLASHATTENTION
📄 THE BASICS
Full Title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
Authors: Tri Dao, Daniel Y. Fu, Stefano Ermon, Atri Rudra, Christopher Ré
Year: 2022
Venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)

One-Sentence Summary: This paper introduced FlashAttention, an algorithm that computes exact attention (no approximation) 2-4x faster and with 5-20x less memory by tiling the computation to minimize reads and writes to GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM).
📖 THE STORY

Tri Dao was a PhD student at Stanford, working with Chris Ré and Stefano Ermon. He was frustrated. Everyone was trying to make attention faster by approximating it: sparse attention, linear attention, kernel methods. But approximations sacrifice accuracy. They change the math. They introduce errors.
Dao asked a different question: What if we don't change the math at all? What if we compute exact attention, but do it in a way that's faster on the actual hardware?

This is a systems-level insight, not a mathematical one. Dao realized that the bottleneck in attention is not the computation (the multiply-adds). Modern GPUs can do trillions of multiply-adds per second. The bottleneck is memory access: reading data from slow GPU memory (HBM) into fast on-chip memory (SRAM), computing, and writing the results back.
A standard attention implementation:
Reads Q, K, V from HBM to SRAM.
Computes the full n × n attention matrix.
Writes the n × n matrix back to HBM.
Reads the n × n matrix from HBM to SRAM.
Applies softmax.
Writes the softmax result back to HBM.
Reads the softmax result from HBM to SRAM.
Multiplies by V.
Writes the final output back to HBM.
That's a lot of reading and writing. The n × n matrix is read and written multiple times. For large n, this dominates the runtime.

Dao's insight: Don't materialize the n × n matrix. Instead, split Q, K, V into small blocks that fit in SRAM. Compute attention block by block. Accumulate the results. Never write the full n × n matrix to HBM.
This is called tiling. And it's the key insight behind FlashAttention.

When the paper was published in 2022, it was a revelation. FlashAttention made exact attention 2-4x faster and used 5-20x less memory. It was adopted by virtually every major LLM training pipeline within months. PyTorch integrated it as a built-in function. It became the default attention implementation in the world.
🔍 THE METHOD — EXPLAINED IN DETAIL
FlashAttention has three key innovations:
Tiling. Split Q, K, V into small blocks of size B_r × d and B_c × d, where B_r and B_c are chosen to fit in SRAM (typically 64 or 128). Process the attention computation block by block.
For each block of Q:
Load the Q block into SRAM.
For each block of K and V:
Load the K and V blocks into SRAM.
Compute the partial attention scores (Q_block × K_block^T).
Apply softmax to the partial scores.
Multiply by V_block and accumulate the result.
Write the final accumulated output to HBM.
The full n × n attention matrix is never materialized. Only small B_r × B_c blocks are ever in SRAM at a time.

Online Softmax. Standard softmax requires knowing the maximum value across the entire row before computing the exponentials. But with tiling, we process the row in blocks. FlashAttention uses an online softmax algorithm that maintains a running maximum and a running sum of exponentials, updating them as each block is processed.

IO-Awareness. The entire algorithm is designed to minimize the number of reads and writes to HBM. The number of HBM accesses is reduced from O(n²) to O(n² / M), where M is the size of SRAM. For a typical GPU with M = 100 KB of SRAM, this is a 100x reduction in memory traffic.
Analogy 1: The Filing Cabinet vs. The Desk.

Standard attention is like a worker who has a tiny desk (SRAM) and a massive filing cabinet (HBM). For every calculation, they walk to the filing cabinet, pull out a file, walk back to the desk, do the calculation, walk back to the filing cabinet, store the result, and repeat. They spend most of their time walking, not calculating.

FlashAttention is like a worker who pulls out a stack of files that fit on the desk, does all the calculations for that stack at the desk, and then files the results once. They minimize the walking. The calculations are the same; the filing is more efficient.
Analogy 2: The Assembly Line vs. The Workshop.

Standard attention is like a workshop where every part is stored in a warehouse across town. For each step, the worker drives to the warehouse, picks up a part, drives back, assembles it, drives back to store the intermediate result, and repeats.

FlashAttention is like an assembly line where all the parts for one batch are delivered to the workstation at once. The worker assembles the entire batch without leaving the workstation. The assembly steps are the same; the logistics are better.

📝 TL;DR: FlashAttention computes exact attention (no approximation) by tiling Q, K, V into small blocks that fit in GPU fast memory (SRAM). It processes attention block by block, using online softmax to accumulate results. The full n × n attention matrix is never materialized in slow memory (HBM). This makes attention 2-4x faster and 5-20x more memory-efficient.
🔢 NUMERICAL WALKTHROUGH
Let's walk through how tiling works with a tiny example.
The Setup:
Sequence length n = 8.
Embedding dimension d = 2.
Block size B_r = B_c = 4 (so we have 2 blocks of Q and 2 blocks of K/V).
SRAM can hold one block of Q (4×2), one block of K (4×2), one block of V (4×2), and the partial attention scores (4×4).
Standard Attention (without tiling):
Load all of Q (8×2), K (8×2), V (8×2) from HBM to SRAM.
Compute the full 8×8 attention matrix. (64 elements)
Write the 8×8 matrix to HBM.
Read the 8×8 matrix from HBM.
Apply softmax.
Write the softmax result to HBM.
Read the softmax result from HBM.
Multiply by V.
Write the output to HBM.
Total HBM reads/writes: Q, K, V (3 reads) + attention matrix (1 write + 1 read) + softmax (1 write + 1 read) + output (1 write) = 8 HBM accesses for the n×n matrix.
FlashAttention (with tiling):
Load Q block 1 (rows 0-3) into SRAM.
Load K block 1 (rows 0-3) and V block 1 into SRAM.
Compute partial attention: Q_block1 × K_block1^T → 4×4 scores.
Apply online softmax to the 4×4 scores.
Multiply by V_block1 → partial output for rows 0-3.
Load K block 2 (rows 4-7) and V block 2 into SRAM.
Compute partial attention: Q_block1 × K_block2^T → 4×4 scores.
Update online softmax with the new scores.
Multiply by V_block2 and accumulate with the previous partial output.
Write the final output for rows 0-3 to HBM.
Repeat for Q block 2 (rows 4-7).
The 8×8 attention matrix is never materialized. Only 4×4 blocks are ever in SRAM.
Total HBM reads/writes: Q blocks (2 reads) + K blocks (4 reads) + V blocks (4 reads) + output (2 writes) = 12 HBM accesses, but each access is small (4×2 instead of 8×8).

The Result: For this tiny example, the difference is modest. But for n = 10,000, the standard approach materializes a 100-million-element matrix. FlashAttention never materializes it. The memory savings are enormous: from 200 MB to a few KB.
See? It's the same math. The IDEA of tiling the computation to stay in fast memory is what's brilliant.
📊 KEY RESULTS

This means the model went from being limited to 2,048-token context windows to handling 8,192, 32,768, and eventually 1,000,000+ tokens. In practical terms, it enabled LLMs to process entire books, long documents, and extended conversations.
💡 WHY SHOULD YOU CARE?

FlashAttention is the unsung hero of the LLM revolution. Without it, GPT-4, LLaMA, Gemini, and ChatGPT would be dramatically slower and more expensive. Every time you interact with a modern LLM, FlashAttention is working behind the scenes, making the attention computation fast and memory-efficient. It is the most impactful systems-level optimization in the history of deep learning.
🔗 WHAT IT LED TO

FlashAttention (2022) → Integrated into PyTorch 2.0 → Enabled 100K+ context windows → Inspired FlashAttention-2 (2023) → Inspired FlashAttention-3 (2024, for H100 GPUs) → Became the default attention implementation in virtually all LLM training pipelines.
⚠️ LIMITATIONS AND CRITICISMS
Hardware-Specific: FlashAttention is optimized for NVIDIA GPUs (A100, H100). It requires custom CUDA code and doesn't generalize easily to other hardware (TPUs, AMD GPUs, CPUs).
Implementation Complexity: The tiling and online softmax algorithms are complex to implement correctly. Bugs can lead to subtle numerical errors.
Still O(n²): FlashAttention makes exact attention faster, but it doesn't change the O(n²) complexity. For extremely long sequences (millions of tokens), even FlashAttention becomes slow.
🧠 EXPLAIN IT TO A 10-YEAR-OLD

Imagine you have to multiply two giant lists of numbers. The normal way is to write down every single intermediate result on a huge piece of paper, then read them all back. FlashAttention is like doing the multiplication in small groups, writing down only the final answer for each group, and never writing down the intermediate results. You do the same math, but you save a ton of paper and time. That's FlashAttention. It doesn't change the math. It just does the math more efficiently.
SECTION: PAPER 2: FLASHATTENTION-2
📄 THE BASICS
Full Title: FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Parallelism and Work Partitioning
Author: Tri Dao
Year: 2023
Venue: arXiv preprint / ICLR 2024

One-Sentence Summary: This paper introduced FlashAttention-2, which achieves 2x speedup over FlashAttention by parallelizing over the sequence length dimension and improving work partitioning between GPU warps.
📖 THE STORY

FlashAttention was a breakthrough, but Tri Dao wasn't satisfied. He profiled the algorithm and found that it wasn't fully utilizing the GPU. The GPU has thousands of cores, organized into "warps" of 32 threads. FlashAttention parallelized over the batch and head dimensions, but not over the sequence length. For small batch sizes (common during inference), many GPU cores sat idle.

Dao's insight was to parallelize over the sequence length dimension as well. Instead of having one warp process an entire row of Q, split the row across multiple warps. Each warp processes a subset of the K/V blocks and accumulates partial results. The final output is a reduction across warps.
He also improved the work partitioning within each warp. In FlashAttention, some warps did more work than others, leading to load imbalance. FlashAttention-2 balances the work more evenly.
The result was a 2x speedup over FlashAttention, and a 5-9x speedup over standard PyTorch attention. FlashAttention-2 became the new default in PyTorch and was adopted by all major LLM frameworks.
🔍 THE METHOD — EXPLAINED IN DETAIL
FlashAttention-2 has two key improvements:

Parallelization over Sequence Length. In FlashAttention, the outer loop iterates over blocks of Q. Each block is processed by one warp. For a batch size of 1 and 8 heads, only 8 warps are active. The rest of the GPU (hundreds of warps) is idle.
FlashAttention-2 splits the Q blocks across multiple warps. Each warp processes a subset of the K/V blocks for a given Q block. The partial results are accumulated and reduced at the end.

Better Work Partitioning. In FlashAttention, the work within a warp is divided unevenly. Some threads compute the dot products, others compute the softmax, others multiply by V. This leads to idle threads waiting for others.

FlashAttention-2 reorganizes the work so that all threads are busy at all times. The dot products, softmax, and V multiplication are pipelined, so while one thread is computing a dot product, another is applying softmax, and another is multiplying by V.
Analogy 1: The Factory Floor Reorganization.
FlashAttention is like a factory where each worker builds an entire product from start to finish. If there are only 8 products to build, only 8 workers are busy. The rest stand around.

FlashAttention-2 is like an assembly line where each worker does one step of the process. All workers are busy at all times. The products move down the line, and each worker adds their part. Throughput is much higher.
Analogy 2: The Kitchen Brigade.
FlashAttention is like a kitchen where each chef cooks an entire dish from start to finish. If there are only 8 orders, only 8 chefs are cooking.
FlashAttention-2 is like a kitchen brigade where one chef chops, another sautés, another plates. All chefs are busy at all times. The dishes move through the brigade, and each chef adds their part.

📝 TL;DR: FlashAttention-2 parallelizes over the sequence length dimension (not just batch and heads) and improves work partitioning between GPU warps. This achieves 2x speedup over FlashAttention and 5-9x speedup over standard attention. It became the new default in PyTorch and all major LLM frameworks.
🔢 NUMERICAL WALKTHROUGH
Let's compare the parallelization strategies.
The Setup:
Batch size = 1.
Number of heads = 8.
Sequence length = 1,024.
Block size = 128.
GPU has 108 streaming multiprocessors (SMs), each with 4 warps = 432 warps total.
FlashAttention Parallelization:
Outer loop: iterate over Q blocks (1,024 / 128 = 8 blocks).
Parallelize over: batch (1) × heads (8) = 8 warps.
Active warps: 8 out of 432. GPU utilization: 1.9%.
FlashAttention-2 Parallelization:
Outer loop: iterate over Q blocks (8 blocks).
Parallelize over: batch (1) × heads (8) × Q blocks (8) = 64 warps.
Additionally, each Q block is split across multiple warps for K/V processing.
Active warps: 64+ out of 432. GPU utilization: 15%+.
The Result: FlashAttention-2 keeps 8x more warps active than FlashAttention. The GPU is much better utilized. The wall-clock time is roughly halved.
See? It's the same math. The IDEA of parallelizing over more dimensions is what's brilliant.
📊 KEY RESULTS
💡 WHY SHOULD YOU CARE?

FlashAttention-2 is the current default attention implementation in PyTorch and virtually all LLM training pipelines. If you have trained or fine-tuned a Transformer model in the last two years, you have used FlashAttention-2. It is the engine that powers the LLM revolution.
🔗 WHAT IT LED TO

FlashAttention-2 (2023) → Default in PyTorch 2.1+ → Inspired FlashAttention-3 (2024, optimized for H100 tensor cores) → Enabled 1M+ token context windows (Gemini 1.5, Claude 3) → Remains the foundation of LLM training and inference.
⚠️ LIMITATIONS AND CRITICISMS
Still O(n²): Like FlashAttention, it doesn't change the asymptotic complexity.
Hardware-Specific: Optimized for NVIDIA GPUs. Not portable to other hardware.
Diminishing Returns: The speedup from FlashAttention-2 to FlashAttention-3 is smaller than from FlashAttention to FlashAttention-2.
🧠 EXPLAIN IT TO A 10-YEAR-OLD

FlashAttention was like having 8 chefs cooking 8 dishes. FlashAttention-2 is like having 64 chefs, each doing one step of the cooking process. All the chefs are busy at all times. The food gets done twice as fast. Same recipes, better organization.
SECTION: PAPER 3: LONGFORMER
📄 THE BASICS
Full Title: Longformer: The Long-Document Transformer
Authors: Iz Beltagy, Matthew E. Peters, Arman Cohan
Year: 2020
Venue: arXiv preprint

One-Sentence Summary: This paper introduced Longformer, a Transformer variant that uses sliding window attention (local) combined with global attention on specific tokens, reducing complexity from O(n²) to O(n × w) where w is the window size, enabling processing of documents with 10,000+ tokens.
📖 THE STORY

In 2020, the maximum context length of most Transformer models was 512 tokens (BERT) or 1,024 tokens (GPT-2). This was fine for short sentences and paragraphs, but useless for long documents: legal contracts, scientific papers, books, medical records.
Iz Beltagy and his team at the Allen Institute for AI (AI2) asked: How can we process documents with 10,000+ tokens without running out of memory?

Their answer was Longformer. The key insight was that most tokens don't need to attend to all other tokens. A word in paragraph 5 probably doesn't need to attend to a word in paragraph 50. It only needs to attend to its local neighborhood (the surrounding words) and a few "global" tokens (like the document title or section headers).
Longformer uses two types of attention:
Sliding Window Attention: Each token attends to a fixed window of w tokens on either side (e.g., w = 256). This captures local context.
Global Attention: A small number of "global" tokens (e.g., the [CLS] token, section headers) attend to all tokens, and all tokens attend to them. This captures global context.

The result is an attention pattern that is mostly sparse (local windows) with a few dense rows/columns (global tokens). The complexity is O(n × w + n × g), where g is the number of global tokens. Since w and g are much smaller than n, this is approximately O(n).
🔍 THE METHOD — EXPLAINED IN DETAIL
Longformer modifies the attention mask to create a sparse pattern:
Sliding Window (Local Attention): For each token i, the attention mask allows it to attend to tokens in the range [i - w/2, i + w/2]. All other positions are masked (set to -∞ before softmax).

Global Attention: A small set of tokens (e.g., the [CLS] token at position 0, and any task-specific tokens) are designated as "global." These tokens attend to all positions, and all positions attend to them.

Dilated Sliding Window (Optional): To increase the receptive field without increasing the window size, Longformer can use dilated windows: attend to every k-th token within the window. This is similar to dilated convolutions in WaveNet (Chapter 11).
Analogy 1: The Neighborhood Watch.
Standard attention is like a town meeting where every resident discusses every issue with every other resident. With 10,000 residents, the meeting never ends.

Longformer is like a neighborhood watch. Each resident only talks to their immediate neighbors (sliding window). But the mayor (global token) talks to everyone, and everyone can talk to the mayor. Local issues are handled locally. Global issues are handled by the mayor.
Analogy 2: The Reading Group.
Standard attention is like a reading group where every member discusses every paragraph of a 500-page book with every other member.

Longformer is like a reading group where each member discusses their assigned chapter with the members reading the adjacent chapters (local). The professor (global token) reads the whole book and can answer questions from any member.

📝 TL;DR: Longformer uses sliding window attention (each token attends to w neighbors) plus global attention (a few tokens attend to everything). This reduces complexity from O(n²) to O(n × w), enabling processing of 10,000+ token documents. It's like a neighborhood watch: local issues are handled locally, global issues by the mayor.
🔢 NUMERICAL WALKTHROUGH
Let's visualize the attention mask for a sequence of 8 tokens with window size w = 2 and global token at position 0.
Standard Attention Mask (all 1s):
Total connections: 64 (n²).
Longformer Attention Mask (window=2, global=token 0):

Token: 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 0: [ 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 ] ← global: attends to all 1: [ 1 1 1 0 0 0 0 0 ] ← local: attends to 0,1,2 2: [ 1 1 1 1 0 0 0 0 ] ← local: attends to 1,2,3 3: [ 0 1 1 1 1 0 0 0 ] ← local: attends to 2,3,4 4: [ 0 0 1 1 1 1 0 0 ] ← local: attends to 3,4,5 5: [ 0 0 0 1 1 1 1 0 ] ← local: attends to 4,5,6 6: [ 0 0 0 0 1 1 1 1 ] ← local: attends to 5,6,7 7: [ 0 0 0 0 0 1 1 1 ] ← local: attends to 6,7
Total connections: 8 (global row) + 7×3 (local) = 8 + 21 = 29 (vs. 64 for standard).
For n = 10,000 and w = 256:
Standard: 10,000² = 100,000,000 connections.
Longformer: 10,000 × 256 + 10,000 × 1 = 2,570,000 connections.
Reduction: 39x fewer connections.
See? It's just masking. The IDEA of local + global attention is what's brilliant.
📊 KEY RESULTS
💡 WHY SHOULD YOU CARE?

Longformer was one of the first practical solutions for long-document NLP. It enabled applications like legal document analysis, scientific paper summarization, and medical record processing. Its sliding window + global attention pattern influenced the design of subsequent long-context models.
🔗 WHAT IT LED TO
Longformer (2020) → Inspired Big Bird (2020, added random attention) → Influenced the design of long-context LLMs → Its sliding window pattern is used in Mistral 7B (2023) and other efficient models.
⚠️ LIMITATIONS AND CRITICISMS
Fixed Window: The window size is a hyperparameter. Too small, and the model misses long-range dependencies. Too large, and the computational cost increases.
Global Token Selection: Choosing which tokens are "global" requires task-specific knowledge.
Superseded by FlashAttention: For sequences up to ~32K tokens, FlashAttention with full attention is now faster and more accurate than Longformer's sparse attention.
🧠 EXPLAIN IT TO A 10-YEAR-OLD

Imagine you are in a school with 10,000 students. In standard attention, every student talks to every other student. That's 100 million conversations! In Longformer, each student only talks to the 10 students sitting next to them (local). But the principal (global token) talks to everyone. Now there are only 100,000 conversations. Much more manageable. And the principal makes sure the important information gets to everyone.
SECTION: PAPER 4: BIG BIRD
📄 THE BASICS
Full Title: Big Bird: Transformers for Longer Sequences
Authors: Manzil Zaheer, Guru Guruganesh, Kumar Avinava Dubey, Joshua Ainslie, Chris Alberti, Santiago Ontanon, Philip Pham, Anirudh Ravula, Qifan Wang, Li Yang, Amr Ahmed
Year: 2020
Venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)

One-Sentence Summary: This paper introduced Big Bird, a sparse attention model that combines sliding window attention, global attention, and random attention, achieving O(n) complexity while preserving the theoretical expressiveness of full attention.
📖 THE STORY
Big Bird was published by a large team at Google, just a few months after Longformer. It addressed the same problem (long sequences) but added a crucial ingredient: random attention.

The authors noticed that Longformer's sliding window + global attention pattern could miss important long-range connections that fall outside the window and aren't captured by global tokens. What if two tokens that are far apart in the sequence are semantically related? The sliding window won't connect them. The global tokens might not capture the specific relationship.

Big Bird's solution: add random connections. Each token attends to a small number of randomly chosen tokens, in addition to its local window and the global tokens. This ensures that, with high probability, any two tokens in the sequence are connected by a short path through the attention graph.

The authors proved theoretically that Big Bird preserves the Turing completeness of full attention: it can compute any function that a full-attention Transformer can compute, given enough layers. This was a strong theoretical guarantee that sparse attention doesn't sacrifice expressiveness.
🔍 THE METHOD — EXPLAINED IN DETAIL
Big Bird's attention pattern has three components:
Sliding Window (Local): Same as Longformer. Each token attends to w neighbors.
Global Tokens: Same as Longformer. A small set of tokens attend to all positions.
Random Connections: Each token attends to r randomly chosen tokens. The random connections are sampled once at the beginning of training and fixed.
The total number of connections per token is: w (local) + g (global) + r (random). The total complexity is O(n × (w + g + r)), which is O(n) since w, g, and r are constants.
Analogy 1: The Social Network.
Local attention is like your close friends and family. You talk to them every day.
Global attention is like celebrities or influencers. Everyone follows them, and they broadcast to everyone.

Random attention is like random acquaintances. You met them at a party, at a conference, on a plane. You don't talk to them often, but they connect you to parts of the world you wouldn't otherwise reach. Together, these three types of connections ensure that information can flow from anyone to anyone in the network.
Analogy 2: The Newspaper.
Local attention is the local news section. You read about events in your neighborhood.
Global attention is the national/international news. Everyone reads the same headlines.

Random attention is the "interesting stories" section. Random, surprising articles from around the world that you wouldn't have found otherwise. Together, they give you a comprehensive view of the world.

📝 TL;DR: Big Bird combines sliding window (local), global tokens, and random connections. The random connections ensure that any two tokens are connected by a short path, preserving the theoretical expressiveness of full attention. Complexity is O(n × (w + g + r)), which is linear in n.
🔢 NUMERICAL WALKTHROUGH
Let's compare the attention patterns of Longformer and Big Bird for a sequence of 8 tokens.
Longformer (window=2, global=token 0):
Total connections: 29.
Big Bird (window=2, global=token 0, random=1 per token): Suppose the random connections are: 1→5, 2→7, 3→6, 4→1, 5→3, 6→2, 7→4.
Total connections: 29 + 7 = 36 (vs. 64 for full attention).

The random connections create "shortcuts" across the sequence. Token 1 can now reach token 5 directly, instead of going through tokens 2, 3, 4. This reduces the maximum path length and improves information flow.
See? It's just adding a few random 1s to the mask. The IDEA of random shortcuts is what's brilliant.
📊 KEY RESULTS
💡 WHY SHOULD YOU CARE?

Big Bird provided the theoretical foundation for sparse attention. It proved that you don't need full O(n²) attention to preserve the expressiveness of Transformers. This insight influenced the design of all subsequent efficient attention models.
🔗 WHAT IT LED TO
Big Bird (2020) → Proved sparse attention preserves expressiveness → Influenced the design of long-context models → Its random attention idea inspired subsequent work on learned sparse patterns.
⚠️ LIMITATIONS AND CRITICISMS
Random is Random: The random connections are fixed at the start of training. They may not be optimal for the specific task.
Implementation Complexity: Implementing the sparse attention pattern efficiently requires custom CUDA kernels.
Superseded by FlashAttention: For sequences up to ~32K tokens, FlashAttention with full attention is now faster and simpler.
🧠 EXPLAIN IT TO A 10-YEAR-OLD

Longformer is like a school where you only talk to your neighbors and the principal. Big Bird adds one more rule: each student also gets one random pen pal from across the school. Now, even if you're in class 1 and your friend is in class 100, you can still send them a message through your pen pal network. The random pen pals make sure no one is isolated.
SECTION: PAPER 5: LINFORMER
📄 THE BASICS
Full Title: Linformer: Self-Attention with Linear Complexity
Authors: Sinong Wang, Belinda Z. Li, Madian Khabsa, Han Fang, Hao Ma
Year: 2020
Venue: arXiv preprint

One-Sentence Summary: This paper introduced Linformer, which projects the Key and Value matrices to a lower dimension (k << n) before computing attention, reducing complexity from O(n²) to O(n × k) while preserving most of the accuracy.
📖 THE STORY

While Longformer and Big Bird reduced attention complexity by making the attention pattern sparse (fewer connections), a team at Facebook AI Research took a different approach: low-rank approximation.

Their insight was based on an empirical observation: the n × n attention matrix is approximately low-rank. Most of the information in the attention matrix is captured by a small number of dominant patterns. The rest is noise.

If the attention matrix is low-rank, you don't need to compute all n² entries. You can project the Key and Value matrices from dimension n to a smaller dimension k (e.g., k = 256), compute the attention in the reduced space, and get a good approximation of the full attention.
This is like compressing a 4K image to a thumbnail before comparing it to another image. You lose some detail, but the overall structure is preserved. And the comparison is much faster.
🔍 THE METHOD — EXPLAINED IN DETAIL
Linformer modifies the attention computation as follows:
Standard Attention:
Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q × K^T / √d) × V
Q is n × d, K is n × d, V is n × d.
K^T is d × n. Q × K^T is n × n. Complexity: O(n² × d).
Linformer Attention:
Project K and V to dimension k: K' = E × K, V' = F × V
E is k × n (learned projection matrix).
F is k × n (learned projection matrix).
K' is k × d. V' is k × d.
Attention(Q, K', V') = softmax(Q × K'^T / √d) × V'
Q is n × d. K'^T is d × k. Q × K'^T is n × k. Complexity: O(n × k × d).
Since k << n (e.g., k = 256, n = 10,000), the complexity is reduced from O(n²) to O(n × k), which is approximately O(n).
Analogy 1: The Summary.
Standard attention is like reading a 100-page book and comparing every page to every other page.

Linformer is like first summarizing the 100-page book into a 10-page summary, then comparing the summary to the original. You lose some detail, but the main ideas are preserved. And the comparison is 10x faster.
Analogy 2: The Thumbnail.
Standard attention is like comparing two 4K images pixel by pixel. 8 million pixels × 8 million pixels = 64 trillion comparisons.

Linformer is like resizing both images to 256×256 thumbnails, then comparing the thumbnails. 65,000 pixels × 65,000 pixels = 4 billion comparisons. 16,000x faster. The thumbnails capture the overall structure, even if they lose fine details.

📝 TL;DR: Linformer projects the Key and Value matrices from dimension n to a smaller dimension k (e.g., 256) using learned projection matrices. Attention is computed in the reduced space, reducing complexity from O(n²) to O(n × k). It's like comparing thumbnails instead of full-resolution images.
🔢 NUMERICAL WALKTHROUGH
Let's walk through Linformer's projection with actual numbers.
The Setup:
Sequence length n = 8.
Embedding dimension d = 2.
Projected dimension k = 3.
Step 1: Project K to K'. K' = E × K (3 × 8) × (8 × 2) = (3 × 2)
(Similarly for K'[1] and K'[2])
Step 2: Compute attention with K' instead of K.
Standard: Q × K^T → n × n = 8 × 8 = 64 entries.
Linformer: Q × K'^T → n × k = 8 × 3 = 24 entries.
The Result: The attention matrix is reduced from 8 × 8 = 64 entries to 8 × 3 = 24 entries. For n = 10,000 and k = 256, the reduction is from 100,000,000 entries to 2,560,000 entries. A 39x reduction.
See? It's just matrix multiplication. The IDEA of projecting to a lower dimension is what's brilliant.
📊 KEY RESULTS
💡 WHY SHOULD YOU CARE?

Linformer demonstrated that the attention matrix is approximately low-rank, a insight that influenced subsequent work on efficient attention. Its simplicity made it a popular baseline for comparing efficient attention methods.
🔗 WHAT IT LED TO
Linformer (2020) → Demonstrated low-rank structure of attention → Inspired subsequent low-rank attention methods → Influenced the design of efficient Transformers for edge devices.
⚠️ LIMITATIONS AND CRITICISMS
Fixed k: The projection dimension k is fixed for all layers and all heads. Different layers may need different k values.
Accuracy Loss: The low-rank approximation loses some fine-grained attention patterns, leading to slightly lower accuracy than full attention.
Superseded by FlashAttention: For most practical sequence lengths, FlashAttention with full attention is now faster and more accurate.
🧠 EXPLAIN IT TO A 10-YEAR-OLD

Imagine you have a giant jigsaw puzzle with 10,000 pieces. To compare it to another puzzle, you'd normally compare every piece to every other piece. That's 100 million comparisons! Linformer is like first taking a photo of the puzzle and shrinking it to a tiny thumbnail. Now you compare the thumbnails instead. Only 256 comparisons. You lose some detail, but you can still tell if the puzzles are similar. And it's way faster.
SECTION: PAPER 6: PERFORMERS (FAVOR+)
📄 THE BASICS
Full Title: Rethinking Attention with Performers

Authors: Krzysztof Choromanski, Valerii Likhosherstov, David Dohan, Xingyou Song, Andreea Gane, Tamas Sarlos, Peter Hawkins, Jared Davis, Afroz Mohiuddin, Lukasz Kaiser, David Belanger, Lucy Colwell, Adrian Weller
Year: 2020
Venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR)

One-Sentence Summary: This paper introduced Performers, which approximate softmax attention using kernel methods (FAVOR+: Fast Attention Via positive Orthogonal Random features), achieving O(n) complexity without explicitly computing the n × n attention matrix.
📖 THE STORY
While Longformer, Big Bird, and Linformer all modified the attention pattern or the attention matrices, a team at Google Brain took a completely different approach: kernel approximation.
Their insight was mathematical. The softmax attention function can be written as:
Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QK^T) × V = D^{-1} × exp(QK^T) × V

Where D is a diagonal matrix of row sums. The key observation is that exp(QK^T) is a kernel function: it measures the similarity between Q and K. And kernel functions can be approximated using random feature maps.
Instead of computing the n × n matrix exp(QK^T) explicitly, you can approximate it as:
exp(QK^T) ≈ φ(Q) × φ(K)^T

Where φ is a random feature map that transforms each d-dimensional vector into a higher-dimensional space. The magic is that you can compute φ(Q) × φ(K)^T × V without ever materializing the n × n matrix:
φ(Q) × (φ(K)^T × V)
First compute φ(K)^T × V (d × d matrix), then multiply by φ(Q) (n × d). The complexity is O(n × d²), which is linear in n.
This is called FAVOR+ (Fast Attention Via positive Orthogonal Random features). And the models that use it are called Performers.
🔍 THE METHOD — EXPLATED IN DETAIL
The Kernel Trick: The softmax attention can be decomposed as:
Attention_i = Σ_j [exp(q_i · k_j) / Σ_l exp(q_i · k_l)] × v_j
The numerator is Σ_j exp(q_i · k_j) × v_j. This is a kernel sum: for each query q_i, compute the kernel similarity with all keys k_j, weight the values v_j by the similarity, and sum.
The Random Feature Approximation: The exponential kernel exp(q · k) can be approximated as:
exp(q · k) ≈ E_ω[ξ(q, ω) × ξ(k, ω)]
Where ω is a random vector sampled from a specific distribution, and ξ is a feature map. By sampling m random vectors ω_1, ..., ω_m, we get:
exp(q · k) ≈ (1/m) × Σ_r ξ(q, ω_r) × ξ(k, ω_r) = φ(q)^T × φ(k)
Where φ(q) = [ξ(q, ω_1), ..., ξ(q, ω_m)] / √m.
The Linear Attention Computation:
Standard: softmax(QK^T) × V → O(n² × d)
Performer: φ(Q) × (φ(K)^T × V) → O(n × m × d)
Since m (the number of random features) is a constant (e.g., 256), the complexity is O(n × d), which is linear in n.
Analogy 1: The Sketch Artist.
Standard attention is like a portrait artist who paints a detailed, pixel-perfect portrait of every person in a room. For 1,000 people, that's 1,000 detailed portraits.

Performers are like a sketch artist who draws a quick, rough sketch of each person. The sketches capture the essential features (the "kernel") without the fine details. The sketches are much faster to draw, and they're good enough for most purposes.
Analogy 2: The Approximation.
Standard attention is like calculating the exact value of π: 3.14159265358979...
Performers are like using the approximation 22/7 = 3.142857... It's not exact, but it's close enough for most practical purposes. And it's much easier to compute.

📝 TL;DR: Performers approximate softmax attention using kernel methods (FAVOR+). Instead of computing the n × n attention matrix, they approximate it as φ(Q) × φ(K)^T, where φ is a random feature map. The computation becomes φ(Q) × (φ(K)^T × V), which is O(n) in sequence length. It's like using a sketch instead of a detailed portrait.
🔢 NUMERICAL WALKTHROUGH
Let's walk through the kernel approximation with a tiny example.
The Setup:
Number of random features m = 2.
Step 1: Compute the exact kernel.
Step 2: Compute the random feature approximation. The feature map ξ(x, ω) = exp(ω^T × x - ||x||²/2) (simplified).
Step 3: Compute the approximation.

The Result: The exact kernel value is 2.586. The approximation with m=2 random features is 0.586. Not great! But with m=256 or m=1024 random features, the approximation converges to the exact value. The key insight is that you never need to compute the n × n matrix. You just compute φ(Q) (n × m) and φ(K) (n × m), and then do φ(Q) × (φ(K)^T × V).
See? It's just exponentials and dot products. The IDEA of approximating the kernel with random features is what's brilliant.
📊 KEY RESULTS
💡 WHY SHOULD YOU CARE?

Performers demonstrated that attention can be approximated with kernel methods, opening a new direction for efficient attention research. The FAVOR+ mechanism influenced subsequent work on linear attention and kernel-based Transformers.
🔗 WHAT IT Led To

Performers (2020) → Demonstrated kernel approximation of attention → Inspired subsequent linear attention methods (cosFormer, ReLU attention) → Influenced the design of efficient Transformers for very long sequences.
⚠️ LIMITATIONS AND CRITICISMS
Approximation Error: The random feature approximation introduces errors, especially for attention patterns with sharp peaks. Accuracy is lower than exact attention.
Random Features Overhead: The number of random features m must be large (256+) for a good approximation, adding computational overhead.
Superseded by FlashAttention: For most practical sequence lengths, FlashAttention with exact attention is now faster and more accurate.
🧠 EXPLAIN IT TO A 10-YEAR-OLD

Imagine you want to know how similar two pictures are. The exact way is to compare every pixel. That's slow. Performers are like a shortcut: you squint at both pictures and compare the blurry versions. The blurry versions capture the overall colors and shapes, even if they lose the fine details. It's not perfect, but it's fast. And for most purposes, it's good enough.
SECTION: PAPER 7: EFFICIENT TRANSFORMERS SURVEY
📄 THE BASICS
Full Title: Efficient Transformers: A Survey
Authors: Yi Tay, Mostafa Dehghani, Dara Bahri, Donald Metzler
Year: 2020
Venue: arXiv preprint (later published in ACM Computing Surveys)

One-Sentence Summary: This comprehensive survey cataloged and compared all major efficient attention variants (sparse, linear, kernel, low-rank, learned patterns), providing a taxonomy and practical guidance for choosing the right method.
📖 THE STORY

By late 2020, the field of efficient Transformers had exploded. Longformer, Big Bird, Linformer, Performers, Reformer, Sparse Transformer, Routing Transformer—the list kept growing. Each paper claimed to be the best. Each used different terminology. Each had different trade-offs.

Yi Tay and his team at Google decided to bring order to the chaos. They wrote a comprehensive survey that cataloged every efficient attention variant, organized them into a taxonomy, and compared their trade-offs.
The survey identified four main strategies for reducing attention complexity:
Sparse Attention: Reduce the number of connections (Longformer, Big Bird, Sparse Transformer).
Low-Rank Attention: Approximate the attention matrix with a low-rank factorization (Linformer).
Kernel Attention: Approximate the softmax kernel with random features (Performers, Reformer).
Learned Patterns: Learn which connections matter (Routing Transformer, Sinkhorn Transformer).

The survey also compared the methods on multiple dimensions: complexity, memory usage, accuracy, and ease of implementation. It became the definitive reference for researchers and practitioners navigating the efficient Transformer landscape.
🔍 THE METHOD — EXPLAINED IN DETAIL
The survey doesn't introduce a new method. Instead, it provides a structured comparison:
Key insight from the survey: There is no single best method. The right choice depends on the task, the sequence length, the hardware, and the accuracy requirements.

Analogy 1: The Field Guide. The survey is like a field guide to birds. It catalogs every species, describes their habitats, diets, and behaviors, and helps you identify which bird you're looking at. Without the field guide, you're lost in a forest of similar-looking birds. With it, you can quickly find the one you need.

Analogy 2: The Map. The survey is like a map of all the roads to the same destination. Some roads are fast but toll-heavy (FlashAttention: exact but O(n²)). Some are slow but free (Performers: linear but approximate). Some are scenic but winding (Longformer: sparse but fixed window). The map helps you choose the right road for your journey.

📝 TL;DR: The Efficient Transformers Survey cataloged all major efficient attention variants into four categories: sparse, low-rank, kernel, and learned patterns. It compared their complexity, memory, accuracy, and ease of implementation. The key takeaway: there is no single best method. The right choice depends on the task and constraints.
🔢 NUMERICAL WALKTHROUGH
Let's compare the complexity of different methods for a sequence of length n = 10,000 and dimension d = 512.

The Result: Sparse, low-rank, and kernel methods reduce the number of operations by ~39x. FlashAttention doesn't reduce operations, but reduces memory traffic by 2-4x. For n = 10,000, all methods are viable. For n = 1,000,000, only the linear methods (or FlashAttention with sequence parallelism) are viable.
📊 KEY RESULTS
💡 WHY SHOULD YOU CARE?

The Efficient Transformers Survey is the map that helps you navigate the complex landscape of efficient attention. If you ever need to choose an attention mechanism for a specific task, this survey is your starting point. It saves you from reading 30+ papers and gives you a structured comparison.
🔗 WHAT IT LED TO

Efficient Transformers Survey (2020) → Became the definitive reference → Guided the design of subsequent efficient models → Influenced the development of FlashAttention (which the survey didn't cover, as it was published later) → Remains a standard reference in the field.
⚠️ LIMITATIONS AND CRITICISMS
Rapidly Evolving Field: The survey was published in 2020. Since then, FlashAttention, FlashAttention-2, and FlashAttention-3 have become the dominant approach, and the survey doesn't cover them.
No Single Winner: The survey's conclusion ("no single best method") is accurate but unsatisfying. Practitioners want a clear recommendation.
Hardware Dependence: The relative performance of different methods depends heavily on the hardware (GPU model, memory size, batch size). The survey's comparisons are necessarily general.
🧠 EXPLAIN IT TO A 10-YEAR-OLD

Imagine you want to get from your house to the park. There are many roads: the highway (fast but crowded), the back roads (slow but scenic), the bike path (healthy but tiring), the bus (cheap but infrequent). The Efficient Transformers Survey is like a map that shows all the roads, with their pros and cons. It doesn't tell you which road to take. It just helps you decide based on what matters to you: speed, scenery, cost, or exercise.

PART VI: THE AGE OF LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
Part VI Overview: "When Autocomplete Became Intelligence"
🎬 The Day the Machine Wrote Back
In June 2020, a team at OpenAI published a paper about a language model with 175 billion parameters. They called it GPT-3.

The paper included a section of examples that made the AI community stop and stare. The researchers had given GPT-3 a few examples of a task it had never been explicitly trained on, and the model had simply... figured it out.
They showed it three examples of translating English to French:
"sea otter" → "loutre de mer"
"peppermint" → "menthe poivrée"
"plush girafe" → "girafe en peluche"
Then they gave it a new phrase: "cheese" →
GPT-3 responded: "fromage"

No fine-tuning. No gradient updates. No training on translation data. The model had never been taught to translate. It had simply read enough text—45 terabytes of it—to absorb the patterns of both languages. And when shown three examples, it inferred the task and executed it.
This was in-context learning. And it was unlike anything the field had seen before.

The examples kept coming. GPT-3 wrote poems. It wrote code. It answered trivia questions. It summarized legal documents. It generated recipes. It even wrote a short essay about itself, in the style of a Shakespearean sonnet.

The reaction was a mixture of awe, excitement, and existential dread. Was this intelligence? Was it understanding? Or was it just the world's most sophisticated autocomplete, predicting the next token with such statistical precision that the output looked like understanding?
The debate rages to this day. But one thing was clear: the era of Large Language Models had begun. And nothing would ever be the same.

This part of the book is the story of that era. It is the story of how the Transformer, the architecture we explored in Part V, was scaled to billions, hundreds of billions, and trillions of parameters. It is the story of BERT, which taught machines to read in both directions. It is the story of GPT, which taught machines to write. It is the story of scaling laws, which revealed the mathematical relationship between model size, data, and intelligence. And it is the story of the open-source revolution—LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek—that democratized LLMs and brought them to the world.
Let's watch autocomplete become intelligence.
🗺️ The Landscape: The World Before LLMs
To understand why LLMs were so revolutionary, we need to understand what NLP looked like before them.

Before 2018, NLP was a task-specific discipline. If you wanted to build a sentiment analyzer, you trained a model on labeled sentiment data. If you wanted a named entity recognizer, you trained a separate model on labeled entity data. If you wanted a question answering system, you trained yet another model on labeled QA data.

Each task required its own dataset, its own model, its own training pipeline. There was no transfer. No sharing. No generalization. Every model was a specialist, trained for one job and useless for everything else.

This was like a hospital where every doctor is a hyper-specialist. The cardiologist can only treat hearts. The dermatologist can only treat skin. The neurologist can only treat brains. If you have a complex condition that involves multiple systems, you're out of luck. No single doctor can help you.
Then, in 2018, two papers changed everything:

BERT (October 2018): Jacob Devlin and his team at Google showed that you could pre-train a single Transformer encoder on a massive corpus of unlabeled text, using a task called Masked Language Modeling (predict the masked word). Then, you could fine-tune that single model on any downstream task—sentiment, QA, entity recognition—with just a small amount of labeled data. One model, many tasks.

GPT-1 (June 2018): Alec Radford and his team at OpenAI showed that you could pre-train a Transformer decoder on unlabeled text, using a task called autoregressive language modeling (predict the next word). Then, you could fine-tune it on downstream tasks. Similar to BERT, but unidirectional.

These two papers established the pre-training + fine-tuning paradigm. Instead of training a specialist for each task, you train a generalist on massive unlabeled data, then specialize it with a small amount of labeled data.
But the real revolution came two years later, with GPT-3.

GPT-3 showed that you don't even need fine-tuning. You can give the model a few examples of a task in the prompt, and it will figure out the task on its own. No gradient updates. No labeled data. Just examples.

This was in-context learning. And it shattered the pre-training + fine-tuning paradigm. The model wasn't a generalist that needed specialization. It was a generalist that could infer the specialization from a few examples.
The implications were staggering. If a model can learn any task from a few examples, then the model is not a tool. It's a platform. A foundation. A foundation model.
The age of LLMs had begun.
