We will trace the arc from GPT-1 (117M parameters) to GPT-2 (1.5B) to GPT-3 (175B) to GPT-4 (multimodal). We will explore in-context learning, few-shot prompting, and RLHF. We will also explore the open-source revolution: LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek, and the Mixture-of-Experts architecture that challenged the "more compute = better" paradigm. What you'll learn: How autoregressive language modeling works, what in-context learning is, why GPT-2 was "too dangerous to release," how RLHF aligned ChatGPT, and how DeepSeek-V3 trained a 671B parameter model on 2,048 GPUs for a fraction of the cost. The analogy: GPT is the world's most advanced autocomplete. But at sufficient scale, autocomplete becomes understanding. Or at least, it becomes indistinguishable from understanding.

Chapter 17: How Big Should a Model Be? — Scaling Laws We explore the mathematical relationship between model size, data, compute, and performance. We will unpack Kaplan's scaling laws, Chinchilla's insight that most models are undertrained, and the controversial concept of emergent abilities. What you'll learn: The power-law relationship between compute and loss, why Chinchilla showed that GPT-3 was undertrained, and why some abilities (like arithmetic reasoning) only appear above certain model sizes. The analogy: Scaling laws are like a recipe. You need the right ratio of flour (parameters) to water (data). Too much flour and not enough water = dry bread (overfit model). Chinchilla found the perfect ratio.
🔑 Key Concepts Preview
Before we dive into the chapters, let's introduce the core vocabulary of the LLM era.

Masked Language Modeling (MLM) Definition: A pre-training task where random words in a sentence are replaced with a [MASK] token, and the model must predict the original words using context from both left and right. Analogy: A fill-in-the-blank quiz. "The capital of France is ___." You can only answer "Paris" if you understand the whole sentence. BERT learned language by doing billions of these quizzes.

Autoregressive Language Modeling Definition: A pre-training task where the model predicts the next token given all previous tokens. The model reads left-to-right and generates one token at a time. Analogy: Autocomplete on your phone. You type "I'm going to the" and your phone suggests "store" or "park" or "movies." GPT does this, but with 175 billion parameters and 45 terabytes of training data.

In-Context Learning Definition: The ability of a model to learn a new task from a few examples provided in the prompt, without any gradient updates or fine-tuning. Analogy: A chef who has never cooked Thai food before, but reads three Thai recipes and then successfully cooks a fourth Thai dish. They didn't go to culinary school for Thai food. They inferred the pattern from the examples.

Few-Shot / Zero-Shot Prompting Definition: Few-shot: providing a few examples of a task in the prompt. Zero-shot: providing no examples, just the task description. Both rely on in-context learning. Analogy: Few-shot is like showing a child three pictures of dogs and then asking "What's this?" with a fourth picture. Zero-shot is like saying "Find the dog in this picture" without showing any examples first.

RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) Definition: A training technique where human raters rank model outputs, a reward model is trained on the rankings, and the language model is fine-tuned with reinforcement learning (PPO) to maximize the reward. Analogy: Training a chef. First, the chef cooks many dishes. Then, food critics rank them. The chef learns which dishes the critics prefer. Eventually, the chef internalizes the critics' taste and cooks what they'd like without being told.

Scaling Laws Definition: Mathematical relationships (power laws) between model size (N), dataset size (D), compute budget (C), and model performance (loss L). L ∝ N^(-α), L ∝ D^(-β), L ∝ C^(-γ). Analogy: A recipe for baking bread. The quality of the bread depends on the amount of flour (parameters), the amount of water (data), and the baking time (compute). Scaling laws tell you the exact ratio for the perfect loaf.

Compute-Optimal Training (Chinchilla) Definition: The insight that for a given compute budget, there is an optimal ratio of model size to dataset size. Most large models (including GPT-3) are undertrained: they have too many parameters and not enough data. Analogy: A student who buys 100 textbooks but only reads 10 of them. They have the capacity to learn (parameters), but they haven't studied enough (data). Chinchilla says: read all 100 textbooks, or buy fewer textbooks and read them all.

Emergent Abilities Definition: Abilities that are not present in smaller models but appear suddenly in larger models. For example, arithmetic reasoning, code generation, and multi-step logic only emerge above ~100B parameters. Analogy: Water doesn't become "wet" until you have enough molecules. A single H₂O molecule isn't wet. Two molecules aren't wet. But at a certain scale, the property of "wetness" emerges. Similarly, certain cognitive abilities emerge at a certain model scale.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Definition: An architecture where the model has many "expert" sub-networks, but only a few are activated for each input. This allows scaling parameters without scaling compute. Analogy: A hospital with 100 specialist doctors, but each patient only sees 2 of them. The hospital has the expertise of 100 doctors, but the cost of 2. DeepSeek-V3 uses MoE to have 671B total parameters but only 37B active parameters per token.
🧑‍🤝‍🧑 The Human Stories: Geniuses, Leaks, and Paradigm Shifts
The age of LLMs is a story of brilliant individuals, dramatic leaks, and paradigm-shifting insights.

We will meet Jacob Devlin, the Google researcher who created BERT. Devlin was a careful, meticulous engineer who had been working on pre-training for years. When BERT was published, it shattered 11 NLP benchmarks simultaneously. Devlin's reaction was characteristically understated: "We're pretty happy with the results." The understatement of the decade.

We will meet Alec Radford, the quiet, reclusive genius at OpenAI who created the GPT family. Radford is famously private. He rarely gives interviews. He doesn't attend conferences. But his papers—GPT-1, GPT-2, GPT-3, CLIP, DALL-E, Whisper—have shaped the entire field. He is the J.D. Salinger of AI: brilliant, elusive, and enormously influential.

We will witness the GPT-2 controversy. In 2019, OpenAI trained GPT-2 (1.5B parameters) and initially refused to release the full model, citing concerns about misuse (fake news, spam, manipulation). The AI community was outraged. "You can't just withhold a research paper!" But OpenAI stood firm. It was the first time an AI lab had explicitly restricted access to a model on ethical grounds. The debate about AI safety and open access began in earnest.

We will see the LLaMA leak. In February 2023, Meta released LLaMA, a family of open-source LLMs. The models were supposed to be available only to researchers. Within days, the weights were leaked on 4chan and BitTorrent. The leak was a watershed moment. It democratized LLMs. Suddenly, anyone with a gaming GPU could run a state-of-the-art language model. The open-source LLM explosion—Alpaca, Vicuna, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek—was born from that leak.

And we will meet the DeepSeek team, a small Chinese AI lab that shocked the world in 2024-2025. DeepSeek-V3, a 671B parameter MoE model, was trained on 2,048 GPUs for a reported $5.6 million—a fraction of the cost of comparable models. DeepSeek-R1, a reasoning model trained with pure reinforcement learning, challenged the assumption that you need massive supervised datasets to teach models to reason. The "DeepSeek moment" proved that the "more compute = better" paradigm was not the only path forward.
🎯 What You'll Be Able to Do After This Part
By the end of Part VI, you will understand the models that define the current AI era. Specifically, you will be able to:

Explain BERT vs. GPT: You will understand the fundamental difference between BERT (encoder, bidirectional, masked LM) and GPT (decoder, unidirectional, autoregressive LM), and why each is suited for different tasks.

Demystify in-context learning: You will understand how GPT-3 can learn a new task from a few examples in the prompt, without any fine-tuning. You will be able to explain few-shot and zero-shot prompting.
Grasp scaling laws: You will understand the power-law relationship between model size, data, compute, and performance. You will know why Chinchilla showed that GPT-3 was undertrained.
Understand emergent abilities: You will be able to explain why some abilities (arithmetic, reasoning, code generation) only appear above certain model sizes, and why this is controversial.
Explain RLHF: You will understand the three-step process of RLHF (supervised fine-tuning, reward model training, PPO optimization) and how it aligned ChatGPT.

Navigate the LLM landscape: You will understand the differences between GPT-4, Gemini, Claude, LLaMA, Qwen, DeepSeek, and Mixtral. You will know which are open-source, which are proprietary, and which use MoE.

Speak the language of LLMs: You will confidently use terms like masked language modeling, autoregressive, in-context learning, few-shot, zero-shot, RLHF, scaling laws, compute-optimal, emergent abilities, and Mixture-of-Experts in conversation.
🔗 Connections: From Architecture to Intelligence
Part V gave us the Transformer: the architecture, the attention mechanism, the positional encoding, the training tricks. We understood how the machine works.

Part VI shows us what happens when we scale that machine to billions of parameters and train it on trillions of tokens. The Transformer is the engine. The LLM is the car. And scaling laws are the physics that govern how fast the car can go.
This part also sets up crucial bridges to the rest of the book:

Part VII (Generative AI): LLMs are generative models. The autoregressive paradigm of GPT is the same paradigm used by diffusion models (in a different modality). Understanding GPT is the key to understanding DALL-E, Stable Diffusion, and Midjourney.
Part XI (AI Agents): ReAct, Toolformer, and Voyager all use LLMs as their "brain." Understanding LLMs is the key to understanding agents.
Part XII (AI Safety): RLHF, Constitutional AI, and DPO are all techniques for aligning LLMs. Understanding LLMs is the key to understanding alignment.
Part XIII (Reasoning): Chain-of-thought, Tree of Thoughts, and DeepSeek-R1 are all techniques for improving LLM reasoning. Understanding LLMs is the key to understanding reasoning.
Part XIV (Efficiency): LoRA, QLoRA, quantization, and distillation are all techniques for making LLMs smaller and faster. Understanding LLMs is the key to understanding efficiency.
The LLM is the common thread. It is the model that ate the world. And in the next three chapters, we will understand it completely.

In the next chapter, Chapter 15: BERT — Reading in Both Directions, we will explore the paper that started the pre-training revolution. We will see how a simple idea—predict the masked word—changed NLP forever. We will understand why bidirectional context matters, and how one pre-trained model can be fine-tuned for dozens of tasks.
Let's teach machines to read.

chapters.title: BERT — Reading in Both Directions

blocks.text: SECTION 1: CHAPTER OPENING HOOK
Here's a test. Fill in the blank:
"The ___ sat on the mat."
Easy, right? "Cat." You didn't even have to think about it.
But how did you know? You read the words to the left of the blank ("The") and the words to the right of the blank ("sat on the mat"). You used context from both directions to infer the missing word.

Now imagine you could only read left-to-right. You see "The" and then the blank. You have no idea what comes next. It could be "cat," "dog," "president," "spaceship." Without the right context, you're guessing.
This is exactly the problem that plagued language models before 2018.

GPT-1, published a few months before BERT, was a Transformer decoder. It read text left-to-right, predicting each word based on the words that came before it. It was powerful, but it was fundamentally unidirectional. It could never look ahead. It was like a student taking a fill-in-the-blank test who is only allowed to read the left half of the sentence.

ELMo, which we explored in Chapter 10, was bidirectional. It used two LSTMs—one reading left-to-right, one reading right-to-left—and combined their outputs. But ELMo was built on LSTMs, which are slow, sequential, and difficult to scale.
The field needed a model that was:
Based on Transformers (fast, parallel, scalable).
Bidirectional (sees both left and right context).
Pre-trained on massive unlabeled data, then fine-tuned for any task.
In October 2018, Jacob Devlin and his team at Google delivered exactly that. They called it BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers.
And it shattered everything.
Eleven NLP benchmarks. Simultaneously. Not by a fraction of a percent. By massive margins. The pre-training + fine-tuning paradigm was born. And the age of LLMs began.
Let's teach machines to read in both directions.
SECTION 2: THE PROBLEM
To understand why BERT was so revolutionary, we need to understand the state of NLP in 2018.

The Task-Specific Era. Before BERT, NLP was a discipline of specialists. If you wanted to build a sentiment analyzer, you trained a model on labeled sentiment data. If you wanted a named entity recognizer, you trained a separate model on labeled entity data. If you wanted a question answering system, you trained yet another model on labeled QA data.
Each task required its own dataset, its own model, its own training pipeline. There was no transfer. No sharing. No generalization.

This was expensive and inefficient. Labeled data is scarce and expensive to create. Training a model from scratch for each task requires massive computational resources. And the resulting models are brittle: they work well on their specific task, but fail on anything else.

The Transfer Learning Hope. Researchers had long dreamed of transfer learning: train a model on a large, general dataset, then adapt it to specific tasks with small amounts of labeled data. This is how humans learn. You don't learn English from scratch for every new task. You learn English once, and then use it for everything.
In 2018, two papers showed that transfer learning was possible for NLP:

ELMo (February 2018): Pre-trained a bidirectional LSTM language model on a large corpus. The contextual embeddings could be used as features for downstream tasks. Improved accuracy by 10-20% on many benchmarks. But ELMo was based on LSTMs: slow, sequential, hard to scale.

GPT-1 (June 2018): Pre-trained a Transformer decoder on a large corpus using autoregressive language modeling. Could be fine-tuned for downstream tasks. But GPT-1 was unidirectional: it could only look left, not right.
The field was at a crossroads. ELMo had bidirectional context but was slow. GPT-1 was fast but was unidirectional. Could you have both? Could you build a Transformer that reads in both directions?

The challenge was that the standard Transformer encoder uses self-attention, where every token attends to every other token. If you use it for language modeling (predict the next word), the model can "cheat" by looking at the answer. Token 3 can attend to token 4, which is the word it's supposed to predict.
GPT solved this with a mask: token 3 can only attend to tokens 1 and 2, not tokens 4, 5, 6. But this makes the model unidirectional.

BERT's solution was elegant: Don't predict the next word. Predict a masked word. If you mask token 3 and ask the model to predict it, the model can attend to tokens 1, 2, 4, 5, 6—both left and right—without cheating, because the answer (token 3) is hidden.
This is Masked Language Modeling. And it unlocked bidirectional Transformers.
SECTION: PAPER 1: BERT
📄 THE BASICS
Full Title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
Authors: Jacob Devlin, Ming-Wei Chang, Kenton Lee, Kristina Toutanova
Year: 2018
Venue: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (NAACL 2019)

One-Sentence Summary: This paper introduced BERT, a bidirectional Transformer encoder pre-trained on two tasks (Masked Language Modeling and Next Sentence Prediction), which can be fine-tuned for a wide range of NLP tasks, achieving state-of-the-art results on 11 benchmarks simultaneously.
📖 THE STORY

Jacob Devlin was not a flashy researcher. He was a careful, meticulous engineer at Google who had been working on pre-training and transfer learning for years. He didn't give many interviews. He didn't make bold predictions. He just built things that worked.
When BERT was published in October 2018, the results were staggering. BERT shattered 11 NLP benchmarks simultaneously:
GLUE (General Language Understanding Evaluation): 80.5 (previous best: 72.8)
SQuAD (Stanford Question Answering Dataset): 93.2 F1 (previous best: 84.1)
MultiNLI (Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference): 86.7% (previous best: 82.1)

These weren't incremental improvements. They were paradigm shifts. On SQuAD, BERT's F1 score of 93.2 was higher than the human performance of 91.2. A machine was now better at reading comprehension than a human.
Devlin's reaction was characteristically understated. In an interview, he said: "We're pretty happy with the results."
The understatement of the decade.

The name BERT—Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers—was a nod to Sesame Street. (Google's AI team has a tradition of naming models after Muppets.) But the name also perfectly describes the architecture: it's a Transformer encoder that produces bidirectional representations.

BERT's impact was immediate and enormous. Within months, it was integrated into Google Search, improving query understanding for 10% of English searches. It became the default backbone for enterprise NLP systems. It spawned a family of variants: RoBERTa, ALBERT, DistilBERT, DeBERTa, and more.

And it established the pre-training + fine-tuning paradigm that would dominate NLP for the next five years. Train once on massive unlabeled data. Fine-tune on small labeled data. One model, many tasks.
The age of foundation models had begun.
🔍 THE METHOD — EXPLAINED IN DETAIL
BERT has three main components: the architecture, the pre-training tasks, and the fine-tuning process.
The Architecture
BERT uses the Transformer encoder (the left half of the original Transformer from Chapter 13). It does NOT use the decoder.
Two sizes:
BERT-base: 12 layers, 768 hidden dimensions, 12 attention heads, 110M parameters.
BERT-large: 24 layers, 1024 hidden dimensions, 16 attention heads, 340M parameters.
The input to BERT is a sequence of tokens. Each token's embedding is the sum of three components:
Token Embedding: The learned embedding for the word/subword (from WordPiece tokenization).
Segment Embedding: Indicates which sentence the token belongs to (Sentence A or Sentence B).
Position Embedding: The learned positional embedding (similar to the sinusoidal encoding in the Transformer, but learned instead of fixed).
Special tokens:
[CLS]: Prepended to the beginning of every input. The final hidden state of [CLS] is used as the aggregate representation for classification tasks.
[SEP]: Separates two sentences in the input.
Pre-Training Task 1: Masked Language Modeling (MLM)
This is the core innovation. BERT randomly selects 15% of the tokens in the input and "masks" them. The model must predict the original tokens using context from BOTH left and right.
Of the selected 15%:
80% are replaced with the [MASK] token.
10% are replaced with a random token.
10% are kept unchanged.

Why this 80/10/10 split? Because during fine-tuning, the [MASK] token never appears. If the model only ever sees [MASK] during pre-training, it will overfit to that specific token. The 10% random and 10% unchanged force the model to build a robust representation that doesn't depend on the [MASK] token.

Analogy 1: The Fill-in-the-Blank Quiz. Imagine a teacher who gives students a sentence with some words blanked out: "The ___ sat on the ___." The students must fill in the blanks using context from both sides. They can look at the words before AND after each blank. This is MLM. The model learns language by doing billions of these quizzes.
Analogy 2: The Mystery Novel.
Unidirectional (GPT) is like reading a mystery novel from left to right. You try to guess the murderer based on the clues you've read so far. You can never look ahead.

Bidirectional (BERT) is like reading the entire novel first, then going back to understand the clues. You know the murderer is the butler, so when you re-read chapter 3, you notice the butler's suspicious behavior. You use context from both directions.
Pre-Training Task 2: Next Sentence Prediction (NSP)

BERT is also trained to understand the relationship between two sentences. Given a pair of sentences (A, B), the model predicts whether B is the actual next sentence that follows A, or a random sentence from the corpus.
50% of the time, B is the actual next sentence (label: IsNext).
50% of the time, B is a random sentence (label: NotNext).
The [CLS] token's final hidden state is fed into a binary classifier for this task.
Note: Later research (RoBERTa, 2019) showed that NSP is not very useful and can be removed without hurting performance. But it was part of the original BERT design.
Fine-Tuning
After pre-training, BERT can be fine-tuned for any downstream task. The process is simple:
Take the pre-trained BERT model.
Add a task-specific output layer (e.g., a linear classifier for sentiment analysis, a span predictor for QA).
Fine-tune the entire model (all layers) on the labeled task data.
The key insight is that you fine-tune the entire model, not just the output layer. The pre-trained weights are a good starting point, but they are adjusted to fit the specific task.
Analogy: The Medical Residency.
Pre-training is like medical school. The student learns general medicine: anatomy, physiology, pharmacology. They don't specialize yet. They learn the foundations.

Fine-tuning is like a residency in cardiology. The student already knows medicine. They just need to learn the specifics of heart disease. The residency is shorter and more focused than medical school.
BERT's pre-training is medical school. Fine-tuning is the residency. One general education, many specializations.

📝 TL;DR: BERT is a Transformer encoder pre-trained on two tasks: Masked Language Modeling (predict masked words using bidirectional context) and Next Sentence Prediction (predict whether two sentences are consecutive). After pre-training, the entire model is fine-tuned for specific tasks. This is the pre-training + fine-tuning paradigm. BERT shattered 11 NLP benchmarks and established the foundation model approach.
🔢 NUMERICAL WALKTHROUGH
Let's walk through a tiny BERT example with actual numbers.
The Setup:
Sentence: "The cat sat" (3 tokens + [CLS] + [SEP] = 5 tokens).
Vocabulary size: 10 (for simplicity).
Embedding dimension: 4.
We want to do MLM: mask "cat" and predict it.
Step 1: Construct the input.
Tokens: [CLS], The, [MASK], sat, [SEP]
Step 2: Look up embeddings.
Token embeddings (from the learned embedding table):
[MASK] → [0.9, 0.9, 0.9, 0.9] (special learned embedding for [MASK])
Segment embeddings (all Sentence A, so all the same):
Position embeddings (learned, one per position):
Step 3: Sum the embeddings. For the [MASK] token at position 2:
Input = Token + Segment + Position

Step 4: Pass through 12 Transformer encoder layers. Each layer applies multi-head self-attention + feed-forward + residual + LayerNorm. After 12 layers, each token has a rich, contextualized representation.
For the [MASK] token, the final hidden state might be:
This representation encodes the meaning of the masked word, based on context from "The" (left) and "sat" (right).
Step 5: Predict the masked token. The [MASK] token's hidden state is fed into a classification layer (linear + softmax) over the vocabulary:
logits = h_[MASK] × W_vocab + b_vocab
probabilities = softmax(logits)
Suppose the probabilities are:
P(other) = 0.02
The model predicts "cat" with 72% confidence. Correct!
Step 6: Fine-tuning for classification (e.g., sentiment). For a classification task, we use the [CLS] token's final hidden state:
logits = h_[CLS] × W_class + b_class (where W_class is 4×2 for binary classification)
probabilities = softmax([1.2, -0.5]) = [0.85, 0.15]
Prediction: Positive sentiment (85% confidence).

The Result: BERT read the sentence "The [MASK] sat" and predicted "cat" using context from both "The" (left) and "sat" (right). It then used the [CLS] token's representation for sentiment classification. One model, two tasks.
See? It's just embedding lookup, Transformer layers, and a classification head. The math is simple. The IDEA of bidirectional pre-training with masked tokens is what's brilliant.
📊 KEY RESULTS
The improvements were not incremental. On CoLA (linguistic acceptability), BERT improved the score by 25.6 points. On SQuAD, BERT surpassed human performance (91.2 F1).

This means the model went from being a task-specific specialist to a general-purpose language understanding engine. In practical terms, it meant that a single pre-trained model could be fine-tuned for sentiment analysis, question answering, named entity recognition, and textual entailment, all with state-of-the-art performance.
💡 WHY SHOULD YOU CARE?

BERT is the foundation of modern NLP. If you have ever used Google Search (since 2019), you have benefited from BERT. Google integrated BERT into its search engine to better understand user queries, improving results for 10% of English searches.

BERT established the pre-training + fine-tuning paradigm that dominated NLP from 2018 to 2023. Every enterprise NLP system, every chatbot, every text classifier built during this period was likely based on BERT or one of its descendants.

And BERT's core insight—that you can learn rich, bidirectional language representations by predicting masked words—remains fundamental. Modern models like DeBERTa, RoBERTa, and even multimodal models like CLIP build on BERT's foundation.
🔗 WHAT IT LED TO

BERT (2018) → Established pre-training + fine-tuning paradigm → Inspired RoBERTa (2019, removed NSP, more data) → Inspired ALBERT (2019, parameter sharing) → Inspired DistilBERT (2019, 40% smaller, 60% faster) → Inspired DeBERTa (2020, disentangled attention) → Influenced T5 (2019, text-to-text framework) → Established the encoder-based branch of the LLM family tree.
⚠️ LIMITATIONS AND CRITICISMS

[MASK] Token Mismatch: During pre-training, the model sees [MASK] tokens. During fine-tuning, it never does. This creates a train/test mismatch. The 80/10/10 strategy mitigates this, but doesn't eliminate it.
NSP is Not Useful: Later research (RoBERTa, 2019) showed that Next Sentence Prediction doesn't help and can be removed. The model learns sentence relationships from MLM alone.

Encoder-Only (Can't Generate): BERT is an encoder. It can understand text, but it can't generate it. You can't use BERT to write a story, translate a sentence, or have a conversation. For generation, you need a decoder (GPT).
Slow Fine-Tuning: Fine-tuning the entire BERT model (110M or 340M parameters) for each task is expensive. This led to parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA and adapters (Chapter 28).
Maximum Length: BERT's maximum input length is 512 tokens. This limits its use for long documents. (Longformer and Big Bird from Chapter 14 address this.)
🧠 EXPLAIN IT TO A 10-YEAR-OLD

Imagine your teacher gives you a sentence with some words covered up: "The ___ sat on the ___." Your job is to guess the covered words. You look at the words BEFORE the blank ("The") and the words AFTER the blank ("sat on the") to figure it out. You use clues from both sides.

BERT does exactly this, but billions of times. It reads sentences with words covered up, and tries to guess the covered words. By doing this over and over, it learns how language works. It learns that "cat" goes with "sat" and "mat." It learns that "Paris" goes with "France" and "capital."

Then, when you want BERT to do a specific job—like figuring out if a movie review is positive or negative—you just show it a few examples, and it uses everything it learned to do the job. It's like a student who studied really hard for a general knowledge test, and then uses that knowledge to pass any specific exam.
SECTION: CHAPTER SUMMARY AND CONNECTIONS
In this chapter, we explored BERT: the paper that started the pre-training revolution and established the foundation model paradigm.

We saw how BERT solved the bidirectionality problem with Masked Language Modeling: instead of predicting the next word (which requires unidirectional attention), BERT predicts masked words using context from both left and right. This simple insight unlocked the power of bidirectional Transformers.

We walked through BERT's architecture: a Transformer encoder with 12 or 24 layers, fed by token + segment + position embeddings. We saw how the [CLS] token provides an aggregate representation for classification, and how the [MASK] token enables bidirectional pre-training.

We explored the two pre-training tasks: MLM (predict masked words) and NSP (predict whether two sentences are consecutive). We saw how the 80/10/10 masking strategy prevents overfitting to the [MASK] token.

We understood the fine-tuning process: take the pre-trained model, add a task-specific output layer, and fine-tune the entire model on labeled data. One model, many tasks. Medical school, then residency.
And we saw the results: 11 benchmarks shattered. SQuAD F1 of 93.2, surpassing human performance. GLUE score of 80.5, a 7.7-point improvement. The pre-training + fine-tuning paradigm was born.
But BERT is only half the story. BERT is an encoder: it understands text, but it can't generate it. For generation—writing stories, translating languages, having conversations—you need a decoder.

In the next chapter, Chapter 16: GPT — The Model That Ate the World, we will explore the other half of the LLM family tree. We will trace the arc from GPT-1 (117M parameters) to GPT-2 (1.5B, "too dangerous to release") to GPT-3 (175B, in-context learning) to GPT-4 (multimodal). We will explore the open-source revolution: LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek. And we will understand how a simple idea—predict the next token—led to machines that can write, reason, code, and converse.
BERT taught machines to read. GPT will teach them to write.

chapters.title: GPT — The Model That Ate the World

blocks.text: SECTION 1: CHAPTER OPENING HOOK
In August 2020, the New York Times published an opinion essay titled "What the Machines Are Learning." The byline read: "GPT-3, an artificial intelligence language model."
The essay was coherent. It was persuasive. It argued that AI was not a threat to humanity. It quoted Gandhi. It made logical arguments. It had a beginning, a middle, and an end.
Most readers couldn't tell it was written by a machine.

The essay was generated by GPT-3, a language model with 175 billion parameters, trained on 45 terabytes of text. The researchers at OpenAI had given it a prompt: "Write a short op-ed about why AI is not a threat to humans." GPT-3 generated several drafts. The researchers selected the best one, edited it lightly, and submitted it to the Times.
The reaction was a mixture of awe and terror. A machine had written a persuasive newspaper essay. Not a template. Not a mad-libs. A coherent, structured, argumentative essay.

But here's the thing that really shocked the AI community. GPT-3 had never been trained to write op-eds. It had never been fine-tuned on newspaper articles. It had never seen a prompt like "write an op-ed" during training.

It had simply read enough text—books, articles, Wikipedia, code, forums—to absorb the patterns of human writing. And when asked to write an op-ed, it predicted the next token, and the next, and the next, each one conditioned on all the previous ones, until it had produced a complete essay.
This was autoregressive language modeling at scale. And it was the beginning of the end of the world as we knew it.

This chapter is the story of GPT: the model that ate the world. We will trace the arc from GPT-1 (117M parameters, a proof of concept) to GPT-2 (1.5B, "too dangerous to release") to GPT-3 (175B, in-context learning) to GPT-4 (multimodal, aligned). We will explore the open-source revolution: LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek. We will understand Mixture-of-Experts, RLHF, and the global race to build the ultimate language model.
Let's watch autocomplete become intelligence.
SECTION 2: THE PROBLEM

In Chapter 15, we explored BERT. BERT was a revolution in language understanding. It could read a sentence, understand its meaning, and classify it, answer questions about it, or extract entities from it.
But BERT had a fundamental limitation: it couldn't generate text.

BERT is an encoder. It reads input and produces a representation. It can tell you whether a movie review is positive or negative. It can answer a question about a passage. But it can't write a story. It can't translate a sentence. It can't have a conversation. It can't write an op-ed for the New York Times.

For generation, you need a decoder. A model that produces text one token at a time, each token conditioned on all the previous tokens. This is autoregressive language modeling: predict the next word, then the next, then the next.

The idea was not new. Language models had existed for decades. N-gram models predicted the next word based on the previous n-1 words. RNN-based language models (Chapter 11) predicted the next word based on a hidden state. GPT-1 (June 2018) used a Transformer decoder for autoregressive language modeling.

But these models were limited. They were small. They were trained on small datasets. They could generate grammatically correct sentences, but the content was incoherent. They couldn't sustain a narrative. They couldn't follow instructions. They couldn't perform tasks they hadn't been explicitly trained on.

The question was: Can autoregressive language modeling scale? If you make the model bigger, train it on more data, and give it more compute, will it eventually become... intelligent? Will the next-token predictor eventually learn to reason, to translate, to code, to converse?
In 2019, GPT-2 suggested the answer might be yes. In 2020, GPT-3 proved it. And in 2022, ChatGPT brought it to the world.

📄 THE BASICS
Full Title: Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners
Authors: Alec Radford, Jeffrey Wu, Rewon Child, David Luan, Dario Amodei, Ilya Sutskever
Year: 2019
Venue: OpenAI Technical Report

One-Sentence Summary: This paper introduced GPT-2, a 1.5 billion parameter Transformer decoder trained on 40GB of text, which demonstrated that a language model can perform many tasks (translation, summarization, question answering) without any explicit supervision or fine-tuning, simply by conditioning on appropriate prompts.
📖 THE STORY

Alec Radford is the J.D. Salinger of AI. Brilliant, reclusive, and enormously influential. He rarely gives interviews. He doesn't attend conferences. He doesn't post on social media. But his papers—GPT-1, GPT-2, GPT-3, CLIP, DALL-E, Whisper—have shaped the entire field.

In February 2019, OpenAI published a paper about GPT-2, a language model with 1.5 billion parameters trained on 40GB of text from Reddit (WebText). The model could generate coherent, multi-paragraph text on a wide range of topics.

But the paper's most provocative claim was in the title: "Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners." The authors argued that a language model, trained only to predict the next token, implicitly learns to perform many tasks. If you give it a prompt like "Translate English to French: cheese =", it will complete it with "fromage." If you give it "Summarize the following article:", it will summarize. No fine-tuning. No labeled data. Just the prompt.
This was zero-shot task transfer. The model hadn't been trained on translation or summarization. It had just read enough text to absorb the patterns of these tasks.
And then OpenAI did something unprecedented: they refused to release the full model.

Citing concerns about misuse—fake news, spam, manipulation, impersonation—OpenAI released only a smaller version (117M parameters) and withheld the full 1.5B model. It was the first time an AI lab had explicitly restricted access to a model on ethical grounds.

The AI community was outraged. "You can't just withhold a research paper!" "This sets a dangerous precedent!" "Who are you to decide what's safe?" The debate about AI safety, open access, and responsible release began in earnest.

OpenAI eventually released the full model in November 2019, after determining that the risks were manageable. But the controversy had changed the field. The question of AI safety was no longer hypothetical. It was here.
🔍 THE METHOD — EXPLAINED IN DETAIL
GPT-2 is a Transformer decoder (the right half of the original Transformer from Chapter 13). It uses:
Masked self-attention: Each token can only attend to previous tokens (not future ones). This ensures the model generates text left-to-right.
Autoregressive language modeling: The training objective is to predict the next token given all previous tokens: P(x_t | x_1, x_2, ..., x_{t-1}).
Byte Pair Encoding (BPE): A vocabulary of 50,257 subword tokens.
The key insight of GPT-2 is that a language model is implicitly a multitask learner. The training objective (predict the next token) forces the model to learn the patterns of many tasks:
If the training data contains "Translate English to French: X = Y", the model learns translation.
If the training data contains "Q: What is the capital of France? A: Paris", the model learns question answering.
If the training data contains news articles, the model learns to write news articles.
The model doesn't know it's "doing a task." It's just predicting the next token. But the next token happens to be the translation, the answer, or the next paragraph of the article.

Analogy 1: The Improv Actor. Imagine an improv actor who has watched thousands of hours of TV, read thousands of books, and listened to thousands of conversations. They've never been explicitly taught to "do a translation" or "write a news article." But if you say "Translate this to French," they can do it, because they've absorbed the patterns of translation from the data they've consumed. GPT-2 is the improv actor. It has absorbed the patterns of language from 40GB of text, and it can perform any task that follows those patterns.

Analogy 2: The Chameleon. A chameleon changes its color to match its environment. It doesn't "know" what color it should be. It just responds to the visual input. GPT-2 is a linguistic chameleon. If you give it a prompt that looks like a news article, it generates a news article. If you give it a prompt that looks like a poem, it generates a poem. If you give it a prompt that looks like a translation exercise, it generates a translation. It adapts to the context.

📝 TL;DR: GPT-2 is a 1.5B parameter Transformer decoder trained to predict the next token on 40GB of text. It demonstrated zero-shot task transfer: by conditioning on appropriate prompts, it can perform translation, summarization, question answering, and more, without any explicit supervision. OpenAI initially refused to release the full model, citing misuse concerns, sparking the AI safety debate.

Let's walk through autoregressive generation with GPT-2.
The Setup:
Prompt: "The cat"
Vocabulary: {"The", "cat", "sat", "on", "the", "mat", "."} (7 tokens for simplicity).
The model outputs a probability distribution over the vocabulary at each step.
Step 1: Generate the first token.
Input: "The cat"
Model computes: P(next | "The cat")
Output distribution:
P("slept") = 0.15
P(other) = 0.10
Sample (or take argmax): "sat"
Generated so far: "The cat sat"
Step 2: Generate the second token.
Input: "The cat sat"
Model computes: P(next | "The cat sat")
Output distribution:
P("still") = 0.10
P(other) = 0.10
Sample: "on"
Generated so far: "The cat sat on"
Step 3: Generate the third token.
Input: "The cat sat on"
P(next | "The cat sat on")
Sample: "the"
Generated so far: "The cat sat on the"
Step 4: Generate the fourth token.
Input: "The cat sat on the"
P(next | "The cat sat on the")
Sample: "mat"
Generated so far: "The cat sat on the mat"
Step 5: Generate the fifth token.
Input: "The cat sat on the mat"

Sample: "."

The Result: The model generated "The cat sat on the mat." one token at a time. Each token was predicted based on all previous tokens. The model didn't "plan" the sentence in advance. It just predicted the next token, over and over, until it generated a period.
See? It's just conditional probability. The math is simple. The IDEA that predicting the next token at scale leads to emergent task performance is what's brilliant.
📊 KEY RESULTS
💡 WHY SHOULD YOU CARE?

GPT-2 was the first model to demonstrate that language models could be general-purpose task solvers. It planted the seed for GPT-3, ChatGPT, and the entire LLM revolution. It also sparked the AI safety debate that continues to this day: should powerful AI models be released openly, or restricted?
🔗 WHAT IT LED TO

GPT-2 (2019) → Demonstrated zero-shot task transfer → Inspired GPT-3 (2020, 175B params, in-context learning) → Sparked the AI safety debate → Influenced the responsible release policies of all major AI labs.
⚠️ LIMITATIONS AND CRITICISMS
Incoherence over Long Text: GPT-2 can generate coherent paragraphs, but over longer texts, it loses the thread, repeats itself, and goes off-topic.
Factual Errors: The model generates plausible-sounding text, but it has no notion of truth. It will confidently state false facts.
No True Understanding: The model is predicting tokens based on statistical patterns. Whether this constitutes "understanding" is a philosophical question that remains unresolved.
Ethical Concerns: The model can generate fake news, spam, and manipulative text. The decision to withhold it was controversial but prescient.

If GPT-2 was a spark, GPT-3 was an explosion.

Published in May 2020, GPT-3 had 175 billion parameters—100x more than GPT-2. It was trained on 45 terabytes of text: books, Wikipedia, articles, code, forums. It was the largest language model ever built.
But the size wasn't the most surprising thing. The most surprising thing was in-context learning.
The researchers discovered that GPT-3 could perform a new task simply by being shown a few examples in the prompt. No fine-tuning. No gradient updates. No labeled dataset. Just examples.
They called this few-shot learning. And it worked on an astonishing range of tasks:
Translation: Show 3 English-French pairs, then ask for a 4th. GPT-3 translates correctly.
Arithmetic: Show 3 addition problems, then ask for a 4th. GPT-3 adds correctly (for small numbers).
Sentiment: Show 3 positive/negative reviews, then ask for a 4th. GPT-3 classifies correctly.
Code generation: Show 3 Python functions, then ask for a 4th. GPT-3 writes correct code.
Creative writing: Ask GPT-3 to write a poem about recursion. It writes a poem about recursion.

The paper included a section of examples that made the AI community stop and stare. GPT-3 wrote a news article. It wrote a poem. It wrote a recipe. It answered trivia questions. It even wrote a short essay about itself.
The reaction was a mixture of awe, excitement, and existential dread. Was this intelligence? Was it understanding? Or was it just the world's most sophisticated autocomplete?
The debate rages to this day. But one thing was clear: the era of Large Language Models had begun.
🔍 THE METHOD — EXPLAINED IN DETAIL
GPT-3 uses the same architecture as GPT-2 (Transformer decoder, autoregressive LM), but scaled up massively:
Parameters: 175 billion (vs. GPT-2's 1.5B).
Layers: 96 Transformer layers.
Hidden dimension: 12,288.
Attention heads: 96.
Training data: 45 terabytes (Books, Wikipedia, WebText2, Common Crawl).
Vocabulary: 50,257 BPE tokens.
The key innovation is not architectural. It's emergent. At 175B parameters, GPT-3 exhibits abilities that smaller models don't have:
In-Context Learning: The model can learn a new task from examples provided in the prompt. The examples are part of the input sequence, and the model conditions on them to generate the output.
There are three regimes:
Zero-shot: No examples. Just the task description. "Translate English to French: cheese ="
One-shot: One example. "Translate English to French: sea otter = loutre de mer. cheese ="
Few-shot: A few examples (typically 3-5). "Translate English to French: sea otter = loutre de mer. peppermint = menthe poivrée. plush girafe = girafe en peluche. cheese ="

Scaling: GPT-3 demonstrated that performance improves smoothly and predictably with scale. More parameters, more data, more compute → better performance. This is the scaling hypothesis, which we will explore in Chapter 17.

Analogy 1: The Chef Who Infers the Recipe. Imagine a master chef who has cooked thousands of dishes. You show them three examples of a Thai curry they've never made before. They taste it, look at the ingredients, and infer the recipe. Then they cook a fourth Thai curry that's just as good. They didn't go to culinary school for Thai food. They inferred the pattern from the examples. GPT-3 is the chef. The examples in the prompt are the three curries. The model infers the "recipe" (the task) and executes it.

Analogy 2: The Student Who Learns from Examples on the Exam. Imagine a student taking a math exam. The first three questions are solved examples: "2 + 3 = 5. 4 + 1 = 5. 7 + 2 = 9." The fourth question is "6 + 3 = ?". The student looks at the examples, infers that the task is addition, and writes "9." They didn't study addition. They learned it from the examples on the exam. GPT-3 is the student. The prompt is the exam. The examples are the solved questions.

📝 TL;DR: GPT-3 is a 175B parameter Transformer decoder trained on 45TB of text. It demonstrated in-context learning: the ability to perform new tasks from a few examples in the prompt, without any fine-tuning. This was an emergent ability that appeared at scale. GPT-3 can translate, summarize, answer questions, write code, and generate creative text, all from a prompt.

And it was all built on LLaMA.Meta responded by releasing LLaMA 2 (July 2023) under a more permissive commercial license. Then LLaMA 3 (April 2024) with 8B and 70B models. Then LLaMA 4 (2025) with Mixture-of-Experts.The LLaMA family became the foundation of the open-source LLM ecosystem. Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek, and dozens of other models built on LLaMA's innovations.### 🔍 THE METHOD — EXPLAINED IN DETAILLLaMA's key insight was **Chinchilla-optimal training** (which we'll explore in Chapter 17). Instead of making the model bigger, LLaMA trained smaller models on more data.* LLaMA-7B: 7 billion parameters, trained on 1.0 trillion tokens.* LLaMA-13B: 13B params, 1.0T tokens.* LLaMA-33B: 33B params, 1.4T tokens.* LLaMA-65B: 65B params, 1.4T tokens.For comparison, GPT-3 (175B params) was trained on 300B tokens. LLaMA-7B has 25x fewer parameters but 3x more data. And it performs comparably to GPT-3 on many benchmarks.**Architectural Innovations:*** **RMSNorm:** A simplified version of LayerNorm that normalizes only the root mean square, not the mean. Faster and more stable.* **SwiGLU:** A gated activation function that improves performance over ReLU.* **RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding):** Encodes position by rotating the Q and K vectors by an angle proportional to their position. More effective than learned or sinusoidal positional encodings.* **GQA (Grouped Query Attention):** A compromise between multi-head attention and multi-query attention. Multiple query heads share the same key and value heads, reducing memory usage.**Analogy 1: The Open-Source Recipe.** * **GPT-4** is like a Michelin-star restaurant. The food is amazing, but you can't see the kitchen. You can't modify the recipe. You can't cook it at home. You can only order what's on the menu.* **LLaMA** is like an open-source recipe. The recipe is published. You can see every ingredient. You can modify it. You can cook it at home. You can share it with your friends. You can build a restaurant around it.**Analogy 2: The Public Library vs. The Private Collection.** * **GPT-4** is like a private collection locked in a billionaire's vault. Only the billionaire can access it.* **LLaMA** is like a public library. Everyone can access it. Everyone can borrow books. Everyone can learn from them. The knowledge is shared.📝 **TL;DR:** LLaMA is a family of open-source LLMs (7B to 65B params) trained on 1-1.4T tokens. It uses RMSNorm, SwiGLU, RoPE, and GQA. Its key insight is Chinchilla-optimal training: smaller models trained on more data. The leak of LLaMA's weights sparked the open-source LLM explosion, democratizing access to state-of-the-art AI.### 🔢 NUMERICAL WALKTHROUGHLet's walk through RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding) conceptually.**The Setup:*** Two tokens: "cat" at position 0, "sat" at position 1.* Query vector for "cat": q = [1.0, 0.5]* Key vector for "sat": k = [0.8, 0.3]* RoPE rotates each vector by an angle θ proportional to its position.**Step 1: Compute rotation angles.*** For position 0: θ_0 = 0 × base_freq = 0* For position 1: θ_1 = 1 × base_freq = 0.5 (simplified)**Step 2: Rotate the vectors.**Rotation by angle θ: [x, y] → [x×cos(θ) - y×sin(θ), x×sin(θ) + y×cos(θ)]* q_rotated = [1.0×cos(0) - 0.5×sin(0), 1.0×sin(0) + 0.5×cos(0)] = [1.0×1 - 0.5×0, 1.0×0 + 0.5×1] = **[1.0, 0.5]** (no rotation at position 0)* k_rotated = [0.8×cos(0.5) - 0.3×sin(0.5), 0.8×sin(0.5) + 0.3×cos(0.5)] = [0.8×0.878 - 0.3×0.479, 0.8×0.479 + 0.3×0.878] = [0.702 - 0.144, 0.383 + 0.263] = **[0.558, 0.646]****Step 3: Compute attention score.*** score = q_rotated · k_rotated = 1.0×0.558 + 0.5×0.646 = 0.558 + 0.323 = **0.881****The Result:** The attention score encodes both the semantic similarity (dot product of q and k) and the positional relationship (the rotation angles depend on position). Tokens at different positions get different rotations, so the attention score naturally captures relative position.See? It's just rotation and dot product. The math is simple. The IDEA of encoding position as rotation is what's brilliant.### 📊 KEY RESULTS| Model | Params | Tokens | MMLU (5-shot) ||---|---|---|---|| **LLaMA-7B** | 7B | 1.0T | 35.1% || **LLaMA-13B** | 13B | 1.0T | 46.9% || **LLaMA-33B** | 33B | 1.4T | 57.8% || **LLaMA-65B** | 65B | 1.4T | 63.4% || **GPT-3 (175B)** | 175B | 300B | 43.9% |LLaMA-13B (13B params) outperforms GPT-3 (175B params) on MMLU, despite having 13x fewer parameters. The key: more training data (1T vs 300B tokens).### 💡 WHY SHOULD YOU CARE?LLaMA democratized LLMs. Before LLaMA, only a few organizations had access to state-of-the-art language models. After LLaMA, anyone with a gaming GPU could run one. The open-source LLM ecosystem—Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek, and dozens of others—was built on LLaMA's foundation. If you care about open access, transparency, and the democratization of AI, LLaMA is the most important paper of 2023.### 🔗 WHAT IT LED TOLLaMA (2023) → Sparked the open-source LLM explosion → Inspired Alpaca, Vicuna, Koala → Led to LLaMA 2 (2023, commercial license) → Led to LLaMA 3 (2024, 8B/70B) → Led to LLaMA 4 (2025, MoE) → Became the foundation of the open-source LLM ecosystem.### ⚠️ LIMITATIONS AND CRITICISMS1. **English-Centric:** LLaMA 1 was trained primarily on English data. Multilingual performance was limited. (LLaMA 3 and 4 improved this.)2. **Leak Controversy:** The initial leak raised questions about responsible release and intellectual property.3. **No Alignment:** The base LLaMA models are not aligned. They can generate harmful content. Alignment requires additional fine-tuning (RLHF, DPO).4. **Compute Requirements:** Even the 7B model requires a GPU with 16GB+ VRAM for inference. The 65B model requires multiple GPUs.### 🧠 EXPLAIN IT TO A 10-YEAR-OLDImagine a really smart robot that only a few companies can afford. LLaMA is like someone publishing the robot's blueprints for free. Now anyone can build the robot. Anyone can modify it. Anyone can make it better. The robot is no longer locked in a corporate vault. It belongs to everyone. That's LLaMA. It's the open-source robot that changed the world.***## SECTION: PAPER 5: DEEPSEEK-V3 & MIXTRAL — THE MIXTURE-OF-EXPERTS REVOLUTION### 📄 THE BASICS**Full Title (DeepSeek-V3):** DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report **Authors:** DeepSeek-AI **Year:** 2024 **Venue:** arXiv preprint**Full Title (Mixtral):** Mixtral of Experts **Authors:** Albert Q. Jiang, Alexandre Sablayrolles, Antoine Roux, Arthur Mensch, Baptiste Savary, Chris Bamford, Devendra Singh Chaplot, Diego de las Casas, Emma Bou Hanna, Florian Bressand, Gianna Lengyel, Guillaume Bour, Guillaume Lample, Lélio Renard Lavaud, Lucile Saulnier, Marie-Anne Lachaux, Pierre Stock, Sandeep Subramanian, Sophia Yang, Szymon Antoniak, Teven Le Scao, Théophile Gervet, Thibaut Lavril, Thomas Wang, Timothée Lacroix, William El Sayed **Year:** 2024 **Venue:** arXiv preprint**One-Sentence Summary:** These papers introduced Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models that scale total parameters (671B for DeepSeek-V3, 46.7B for Mixtral) while only activating a small subset per token (37B for DeepSeek-V3, 12.9B for Mixtral), achieving state-of-the-art performance at a fraction of the compute cost.### 📖 THE STORYIn December 2024, a small Chinese AI lab called DeepSeek published a technical report that shocked the world.DeepSeek-V3 had 671 billion total parameters. But only 37 billion were active for each token. It was trained on 2,048 NVIDIA H800 GPUs for approximately 2.788 million GPU hours. The estimated training cost: **$5.6 million**.For comparison, GPT-4 was rumored to have cost over $100 million to train. DeepSeek-V3 achieved comparable performance at 5% of the cost.The secret was **Mixture-of-Experts (MoE)**. Instead of one massive network where every parameter is active for every token, MoE has many smaller "expert" networks. For each token, a "router" selects the top-k experts (e.g., top-2 out of 256). Only those experts process the token. The rest are idle.This means you can have 671B total parameters (the sum of all experts) but only 37B active parameters (the experts actually used per token). The model has the knowledge of 671B parameters but the compute cost of 37B parameters.A few weeks earlier, Mistral AI (a French startup founded by former Meta and DeepMind researchers) had released Mixtral 8x7B, a smaller MoE model with 46.7B total parameters and 12.9B active parameters. Mixtral outperformed LLaMA 2 70B (which has 70B active parameters) while using 6x less compute per token.The MoE revolution had begun. The "more compute = better" paradigm was challenged. You didn't need to burn $100 million to train a frontier model. You needed a smarter architecture.### 🔍 THE METHOD — EXPLAINED IN DETAIL**Mixture-of-Experts Architecture:**A standard Transformer feed-forward network (FFN) is a single large network:* FFN(x) = W_2 × ReLU(W_1 × x + b_1) + b_2An MoE FFN replaces the single FFN with N expert FFNs and a router:* Router(x) = softmax(W_r × x) → produces a probability distribution over N experts.* Select top-k experts (e.g., k=2).* Output = Σ_i g_i × Expert_i(x), where g_i are the router's weights for the selected experts.**DeepSeek-V3 Specifics:*** 256 experts per MoE layer.* Top-8 experts selected per token (plus 1 shared expert).* 671B total parameters, 37B active per token.* Auxiliary loss for load balancing (ensures all experts are used evenly).* Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) for efficient KV cache.* FP8 mixed-precision training.**Mixtral Specifics:*** 8 experts per MoE layer.* Top-2 experts selected per token.* 46.7B total parameters, 12.9B active per token.**Analogy 1: The Hospital with 100 Specialists.** * **Standard FFN** is like a hospital where every patient sees every doctor. You have a headache? You see the cardiologist, the dermatologist, the neurologist, the orthopedist—all 100 doctors. Incredibly expensive and slow.* **MoE** is like a hospital with a triage nurse (the router). You have a headache? The nurse sends you to the neurologist and the ophthalmologist (top-2 experts). You don't see the cardiologist or the dermatologist. You get expert care at a fraction of the cost.**Analogy 2: The Restaurant with 50 Chefs.** * **Standard FFN** is like a restaurant where all 50 chefs cook every dish. You order a salad? All 50 chefs work on your salad. Absurdly wasteful.* **MoE** is like a restaurant where a head chef (the router) assigns 2 chefs to each dish. You order a salad? The salad specialist and the dressing specialist make it. You order a steak? The grill specialist and the sauce specialist make it. The restaurant has the expertise of 50 chefs but the cost of 2.📝 **TL;DR:** Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) replaces the single FFN in each Transformer layer with many smaller "expert" FFNs and a router. For each token, the router selects the top-k experts (e.g., 2 out of 256). Only those experts process the token. This allows scaling total parameters (671B) while keeping active parameters small (37B), achieving state-of-the-art performance at a fraction of the compute cost.### 🔢 NUMERICAL WALKTHROUGHLet's walk through the MoE routing with a tiny example.**The Setup:*** 4 experts: E_0, E_1, E_2, E_3.* Top-k = 2 (select 2 experts per token).* Input token representation: x = [0.5, 0.3]* Router weight matrix W_r (4 × 2):
Step 1: Compute router logits.
logits = W_r × x
Step 2: Apply softmax to get router probabilities.
Step 3: Select top-2 experts.
Top-2: Expert 2 (0.261) and Expert 3 (0.261). (Tie broken arbitrarily.)
Step 4: Compute expert outputs.
Expert_2(x) = [0.7, 0.4] (simplified)
Expert_3(x) = [0.3, 0.8] (simplified)
Step 5: Weighted sum.
Output = g_2 × Expert_2(x) + g_3 × Expert_3(x)
The Result: The router selected Experts 2 and 3. Only those two experts processed the token. Experts 0 and 1 were idle. The model has the knowledge of 4 experts but the compute cost of 2.
See? It's just a softmax, a top-k selection, and a weighted sum. The math is simple. The IDEA of sparse expert routing is what's brilliant.
📊 KEY RESULTS
DeepSeek-V3 achieved GPT-4-level performance at 5% of the estimated cost. Mixtral outperformed LLaMA 2 70B with 6x less compute per token.
💡 WHY SHOULD YOU CARE?

MoE challenged the "more compute = better" paradigm. It showed that you can achieve frontier performance without burning $100 million. This democratizes AI research. Small labs, universities, and startups can now train competitive models. DeepSeek-V3 proved that the US-China AI gap is smaller than many assumed.
🔗 WHAT IT LED TO

Mixtral (2024) → Proved MoE works at small scale → Inspired DeepSeek-V3 (2024, 671B MoE) → Inspired DeepSeek-R1 (2025, reasoning with RL) → Influenced LLaMA 4 (2025, MoE) → MoE became the default architecture for frontier models.
⚠️ LIMITATIONS AND CRITICISMS
Memory Requirements: All experts must be stored in memory, even if only a few are active per token. DeepSeek-V3's 671B parameters require ~1.3TB of memory.
Load Balancing: Without careful training, some experts are used more than others, leading to inefficiency. Auxiliary losses are needed to balance the load.
Routing Instability: The router's decisions can be unstable during training, leading to expert collapse (all tokens routed to the same expert).
Complexity: MoE adds architectural complexity. Debugging and interpreting MoE models is harder than dense models.
🧠 EXPLAIN IT TO A 10-YEAR-OLD

Imagine a school with 100 teachers. In a normal school, every student goes to every teacher for every subject. That's slow and expensive. In an MoE school, a counselor (the router) looks at your question and sends you to the 2 best teachers for that topic. You don't see all 100 teachers. You only see the 2 who know the most about your question. The school has the expertise of 100 teachers, but you only use 2 at a time. That's MoE. It's like having 100 teachers but only paying for 2.
SECTION: PAPER 6: PALM, GEMINI, QWEN — SCALING AND MULTIMODALITY
📄 THE BASICS
PaLM: Chowdhery et al. (2022) — PaLM: Scaling Language Modeling with Pathways
Gemini: Google DeepMind (2023-2025) — Gemini: A Family of Highly Capable Multimodal Models
Qwen: Alibaba (2023-2026) — Qwen Technical Report

One-Sentence Summary: These papers represent the global race to build the ultimate multimodal LLM: PaLM scaled to 540B parameters, Gemini unified text/image/audio/video, and Qwen provided a strong open-source multilingual alternative.
📖 THE STORY
By 2022, the LLM race had become a global competition. OpenAI had GPT. Google had PaLM and Gemini. Meta had LLaMA. Anthropic had Claude. Alibaba had Qwen. DeepSeek had V3 and R1. Mistral had Mixtral.
Each lab pushed the boundaries in different directions:

PaLM (2022): Google's 540B parameter model, trained on 780B tokens. PaLM was notable for its exploration of scaling laws and emergent abilities. It showed that some abilities (like arithmetic reasoning) only appear above certain model sizes. PaLM also demonstrated "chain-of-thought" prompting, where asking the model to "think step by step" dramatically improved reasoning performance.

Gemini (2023-2025): Google DeepMind's multimodal family. Gemini 1.0 was trained natively on text, images, audio, and video. Gemini 1.5 introduced a 1-million-token context window using a Mixture-of-Experts architecture. Gemini 2.0 and 2.5 pushed multimodal reasoning and agentic capabilities. Gemini represents Google's attempt to unify all modalities under a single Transformer.

Qwen (2023-2026): Alibaba's open-source model family. Qwen 1.0 was a strong multilingual model. Qwen 2.0 improved coding and reasoning. Qwen 2.5 and 3.x pushed the boundaries of open-source performance, with models ranging from 0.5B to 72B+ parameters. Qwen is notable for its strong multilingual capabilities (especially Chinese-English) and its commitment to open-source release.
🔍 THE METHOD — EXPLAINED IN DETAIL
PaLM's Key Innovations:
Scale: 540B parameters, the largest dense model at the time.
Efficient Training: Used Google's Pathways system for distributed training across 6,144 TPU v4 chips.
Chain-of-Thought: Demonstrated that "Let's think step by step" prompting dramatically improves reasoning.
Emergent Abilities: Documented abilities that appear only above certain scales.
Gemini's Key Innovations:
Native Multimodality: Trained from the start on interleaved text, images, audio, and video. Not a text model with a vision adapter bolted on.
Long Context: Gemini 1.5 supports 1M+ token context windows using MoE and efficient attention.
Mixture-of-Experts: Gemini 1.5 and 2.0 use MoE for efficiency.
Agentic Capabilities: Gemini 2.0 and 2.5 can use tools, browse the web, and execute multi-step plans.
Qwen's Key Innovations:
Multilingual Pre-training: Trained on a balanced mix of Chinese, English, and other languages.
Open Source: All model weights released openly.
Strong Coding and Math: Qwen 2.5-Coder and Qwen 2.5-Math are specialized variants that outperform many larger models.
MoE: Qwen 3.x uses Mixture-of-Experts for efficiency.
Analogy 1: The Polyglot.
GPT-4 is like a brilliant English speaker who has learned some French and Spanish.
Qwen is like a native bilingual speaker who grew up speaking both Chinese and English. The multilingual ability is not an add-on; it's fundamental.
Analogy 2: The Renaissance Person.
GPT-3 is like a brilliant writer who can only write.
Gemini is like a Renaissance person who can write, paint, compose music, and make films. It's not just a language model; it's a multimodal intelligence.

📝 TL;DR: PaLM scaled to 540B parameters and explored emergent abilities and chain-of-thought. Gemini unified text, images, audio, and video in a single natively multimodal model with 1M+ token context. Qwen provided a strong open-source multilingual alternative with specialized coding and math variants. Together, they represent the global race to build the ultimate multimodal LLM.
🔢 NUMERICAL WALKTHROUGH
Let's walk through multimodal tokenization (how Gemini processes an image + text prompt).
The Setup:
Input: An image of a cat + the text "What is this?"
Image: 224 × 224 pixels.
Patch size: 16 × 16 (from ViT, Chapter 9).
Number of image patches: (224/16) × (224/16) = 14 × 14 = 196 patches.
Text tokens: ["What", "is", "this", "?"] = 4 tokens.
Step 1: Tokenize the image.
Split the image into 196 patches of 16×16 pixels.
Each patch is flattened to a 768-dimensional vector (16×16×3 = 768).
Each patch vector is projected to the model's embedding dimension (e.g., 4096 for Gemini).
Add positional embeddings to each patch.
Result: 196 image tokens, each 4096-dimensional.
Step 2: Tokenize the text.
Tokenize "What is this?" into BPE tokens: ["What", "is", "this", "?"].
Look up token embeddings: 4 text tokens, each 4096-dimensional.
Add positional embeddings.
Step 3: Interleave image and text tokens.
Combined sequence: [img_1, img_2, ..., img_196, "What", "is", "this", "?"]
Total: 200 tokens, each 4096-dimensional.
Step 4: Feed to Transformer decoder.
The 200-token sequence is fed into the Transformer decoder.
Each token attends to all previous tokens (masked self-attention).
The model generates the response: "This is a cat."

The Result: The model processed an image and a text question as a single sequence of tokens. The image patches and text tokens are in the same embedding space. The Transformer doesn't know which tokens are "image" and which are "text." It just sees a sequence of vectors and predicts the next one.
See? It's just tokenization and concatenation. The math is simple. The IDEA of treating all modalities as tokens is what's brilliant.
📊 KEY RESULTS
💡 WHY SHOULD YOU CARE?

These models represent the frontier of AI. PaLM showed us that scale leads to emergent abilities. Gemini showed us that multimodality is the future. Qwen showed us that open-source models can compete with proprietary ones. Together, they define the state of the art and point to where AI is heading: multimodal, multilingual, agentic, and increasingly open.
🔗 WHAT IT LED TO

PaLM (2022) → Inspired chain-of-thought research → Led to PaLM 2 and Gemini → Gemini (2023) → Set the standard for multimodal AI → Led to Gemini 2.5 (2025, reasoning) → Qwen (2023) → Became the leading open-source multilingual model → Influenced the global open-source LLM ecosystem.
⚠️ LIMITATIONS AND CRITICISMS
PaLM: Dense 540B model is extremely expensive to train and run. Superseded by MoE architectures.
Gemini: Proprietary. No open weights. Limited transparency.
Qwen: Multilingual performance varies by language. Some languages are underrepresented in training data.
All: Still hallucinate. Still biased. Still lack true understanding (debatable).
🧠 EXPLAIN IT TO A 10-YEAR-OLD

PaLM is like a really smart student who read every book in the library and discovered that if you ask them to "think step by step," they can solve really hard math problems. Gemini is like a student who can read books, look at pictures, listen to music, and watch videos, all at the same time. Qwen is like a student who speaks two languages fluently and shares all their notes with the class for free. Together, they're the smartest students in the world, and they're getting smarter every year.
SECTION: CHAPTER SUMMARY AND CONNECTIONS
In this chapter, we explored the models that ate the world: the GPT family and the LLM revolution.

We started with GPT-2, the 1.5B parameter model that demonstrated zero-shot task transfer and was "too dangerous to release." We saw how autoregressive language modeling—predicting the next token—can implicitly learn to perform many tasks.

We explored GPT-3, the 175B parameter model that demonstrated in-context learning. We saw how a few examples in the prompt can activate the model's pre-existing knowledge, enabling it to perform new tasks without any fine-tuning. We understood the difference between zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot prompting.

We encountered GPT-4, the multimodal, aligned frontier model. We saw how RLHF (supervised fine-tuning, reward model training, PPO optimization) aligns the model to be helpful, harmless, and honest. We saw how multimodality (text + images) extends the model's capabilities.

We witnessed the open-source revolution with LLaMA. We saw how the leak of LLaMA's weights democratized LLMs, sparking an explosion of community-built models. We explored LLaMA's architectural innovations: RMSNorm, SwiGLU, RoPE, and GQA.

We explored the Mixture-of-Experts revolution with DeepSeek-V3 and Mixtral. We saw how sparse expert routing allows scaling total parameters (671B) while keeping active parameters small (37B), achieving frontier performance at a fraction of the cost.

And we surveyed the global LLM race with PaLM, Gemini, and Qwen. We saw how PaLM explored scaling laws and emergent abilities, how Gemini unified all modalities, and how Qwen provided a strong open-source multilingual alternative.

Together, these models transformed AI from a niche research field into a global industry. They power chatbots, code assistants, translation services, image generators, and scientific discovery tools. They are the most impactful technology of the 21st century.
But a crucial question remains: How big should a model be? Is bigger always better? What's the optimal ratio of parameters to data? Why do some abilities only appear above certain scales?

In the next chapter, Chapter 17: How Big Should a Model Be? — Scaling Laws, we will explore the mathematics of scale. We will unpack Kaplan's scaling laws, Chinchilla's insight that most models are undertrained, and the controversial concept of emergent abilities. We will understand the recipe for the perfect model: the right ratio of flour (parameters) to water (data) to baking time (compute).
The models are built. Now, let's understand the physics that govern them.

chapters.title: How Big Should a Model Be? — Scaling Laws

blocks.text: SECTION 1: CHAPTER OPENING HOOK
In 2020, training a frontier language model cost millions of dollars.

GPT-3, with its 175 billion parameters, consumed an estimated 3,640 petaflop-days of compute. At cloud pricing, that's roughly $4.6 million. And that was just the training. The electricity, the hardware, the engineering time—it all added up.
If you're the researcher in charge of the next model, you face a billion-dollar question: How big should the model be?

Make it too small, and you waste your data. The model can't absorb all the information you've fed it. Make it too big, and you waste your money. You're paying for parameters that don't improve performance because you didn't give them enough data to learn from.

Before 2020, this question was answered by intuition and trial-and-error. Researchers would train a model, see if it was good, and if not, make it bigger. There was no theory. No prediction. No way to know in advance whether a 10-billion-parameter model trained on 100 billion tokens would be better than a 100-billion-parameter model trained on 10 billion tokens.
Then, three papers changed everything.

The first, by Jared Kaplan and his team at OpenAI, discovered that model performance follows power laws: smooth, predictable mathematical curves that relate model size, data size, and compute to performance. If you know the curve, you can predict the performance of a model before you train it.

The second, by Jordan Hoffmann and his team at DeepMind, dropped a bombshell: GPT-3 is undertrained. Most large models have too many parameters and not enough data. The optimal ratio is about 20 tokens per parameter. GPT-3, with 175B parameters and 300B tokens, has only 1.7 tokens per parameter. It's like a student who bought 100 textbooks but only read 2 of them.

The third, by Jason Wei and his team at Google Brain, revealed a surprise: some abilities don't improve smoothly with scale. They appear suddenly, like a phase transition. Arithmetic reasoning, code generation, and multi-step logic are near zero for small models and jump to high accuracy above ~100B parameters. These are emergent abilities.
Together, these three papers gave us the physics of scaling. They told us how big to make the model, how much data to feed it, and what surprises to expect along the way.
Let's learn the recipe.
SECTION 2: THE PROBLEM
Training a large language model is an optimization problem with three variables:
N (Parameters): The number of trainable weights in the model. More parameters = more capacity to learn.
D (Data): The number of tokens in the training dataset. More data = more information to learn from.
C (Compute): The total number of floating-point operations (FLOPs) used for training. More compute = more training steps.
These three variables are related. The approximate compute cost of training a Transformer is:
C ≈ 6 × N × D
(The factor of 6 comes from the forward pass, the backward pass, and the optimizer state.)

Given a fixed compute budget C, you have to choose N and D. Make N too big, and D is too small (the model memorizes the data). Make D too big, and N is too small (the model can't absorb all the data). There's a sweet spot.
Before 2020, nobody knew where the sweet spot was. Researchers relied on heuristics:
"Make the model as big as you can afford."
"Train on as much data as you can find."
"If the loss is still going down, keep training."

These heuristics worked, but they were wasteful. GPT-3 was trained on 300B tokens. But was that the right amount? Could a smaller model trained on more data have achieved the same performance? Nobody knew.
The field needed a mathematical framework. A set of equations that relate N, D, C, and performance (loss L). A recipe.
Three papers provided it.
SECTION: PAPER 1: SCALING LAWS FOR NEURAL LANGUAGE MODELS
📄 THE BASICS
Full Title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
Authors: Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, Tom Henighan, Tom B. Brown, Benjamin Chess, Rewon Child, Scott Gray, Alec Radford, Jeffrey Wu, Dario Amodei
Year: 2020
Venue: arXiv preprint

One-Sentence Summary: This paper discovered that language model performance (loss) follows smooth power-law relationships with model size (N), dataset size (D), and compute budget (C), enabling prediction of model performance before training.
📖 THE STORY

Jared Kaplan was a theoretical physicist turned AI researcher at OpenAI. He brought a physicist's intuition to the problem: if you plot the right variables on the right axes, the data should fall on a clean curve.

The team trained hundreds of language models of varying sizes—from 768 parameters to 1.5 billion—on datasets of varying sizes. They measured the cross-entropy loss (how well the model predicts the next token) for each model.
Then they plotted the results. And they saw something beautiful.
On a log-log plot, the data fell on straight lines. This means the relationships are power laws:
L ∝ N^(-α_N): Loss decreases as a power of model size.
L ∝ D^(-α_D): Loss decreases as a power of dataset size.
L ∝ C^(-α_C): Loss decreases as a power of compute budget.
The exponents were small but consistent:
α_N ≈ 0.076 (loss decreases slowly with model size)
α_D ≈ 0.095 (loss decreases slightly faster with data size)
α_C ≈ 0.050 (loss decreases slowly with compute)

The key insight: performance improves smoothly and predictably with scale. There are no sudden jumps. No phase transitions. No magic thresholds. Just smooth, continuous improvement. If you double the model size, the loss decreases by a fixed percentage. If you 10x the data, the loss decreases by a fixed percentage.

This was the scaling hypothesis: the performance of a language model is a smooth, predictable function of N, D, and C. If you know the function, you can predict the performance of a model before you train it. You can extrapolate from small models to large ones. You can plan your training run in advance.
The paper was a revelation. It turned model training from an art into a science.
🔍 THE METHOD — EXPLAINED IN DETAIL
The scaling laws are empirical power-law fits:
L(N) = (N_c / N)^α_N
Where:
L(N) is the cross-entropy loss for a model with N parameters.
N_c is a constant (the "critical" model size where loss = 1).
Similarly:
L(D) = (D_c / D)^α_D, with α_D ≈ 0.095.
L(C) = (C_c / C)^α_C, with α_C ≈ 0.050.
These are power laws: y = a × x^(-b). On a log-log plot, they appear as straight lines with slope -b.
Key findings:

Model size matters more than data size (for fixed compute). If you have a fixed compute budget, it's better to make the model bigger and train on less data than to make the model smaller and train on more data. (This was later corrected by Chinchilla.)

Width, depth, and attention heads scale similarly. The power law holds regardless of whether you increase width (hidden dimension), depth (number of layers), or attention heads. Total parameters is what matters.
The power laws hold across 7 orders of magnitude. From 768 parameters to 1.5 billion, the curves are smooth and predictable.
Analogy 1: The Recipe.
N (parameters) is the amount of flour.
D (data) is the amount of water.
C (compute) is the baking time.
L (loss) is how good the bread tastes.

The scaling laws are the recipe. They tell you: if you double the flour, the bread gets 5% better. If you double the water, the bread gets 7% better. If you double the baking time, the bread gets 3% better. You can predict the taste of the bread before you bake it.
Analogy 2: The Car Engine.
N is the horsepower of the engine.
D is the amount of fuel in the tank.
C is the driving time.
L is how fast you reach your destination.

More horsepower makes you faster, but with diminishing returns. Going from 100 to 200 horsepower is a big improvement. Going from 1,000 to 1,100 horsepower is barely noticeable. The scaling laws tell you exactly how much faster you'll go for each additional horsepower.

📝 TL;DR: Scaling laws are power-law relationships between model performance (loss) and model size (N), dataset size (D), and compute budget (C). Loss decreases smoothly and predictably as N, D, and C increase. The exponents are small (0.05-0.10), meaning you need 10x more resources to get a fixed percentage improvement. The scaling laws allow you to predict model performance before training.
