Let's use the scaling laws to predict model performance.
The Setup:
Scaling law: L(N) = (N_c / N)^0.076
Let's say N_c = 10^10 (a constant fitted from data).
We want to predict the loss for models of different sizes.
Step 1: Model with N = 10^8 (100M parameters).
Step 2: Model with N = 10^9 (1B parameters).
Step 3: Model with N = 10^10 (10B parameters).
Step 4: Model with N = 10^11 (100B parameters).
The Result:
Notice the pattern: every 10x increase in model size reduces the loss by a factor of ~0.84 (a 16% improvement). This is the power law. The improvement is smooth, predictable, and consistent.
If you're planning a training run and you know the loss of a 1B model, you can predict the loss of a 100B model without training it. You just extrapolate along the power law.
See? It's just exponents and logarithms. The math is simple. The IDEA that performance follows a smooth, predictable curve is what's brilliant.
📊 KEY RESULTS
💡 WHY SHOULD YOU CARE?

Scaling laws turned model training from an art into a science. Before scaling laws, researchers trained models by trial-and-error. After scaling laws, they could plan their training runs in advance, predict performance, and allocate resources efficiently. Every major AI lab uses scaling laws to plan their training runs. If you've ever wondered how OpenAI knew GPT-4 would be good before they trained it, the answer is scaling laws.
🔗 WHAT IT LED TO

Scaling Laws (2020) → Established the scaling hypothesis → Inspired Chinchilla (2022, corrected the N/D ratio) → Inspired the "bigger is better" era of AI → Guided the training of GPT-3, GPT-4, PaLM, LLaMA, and all frontier models → Became the foundation of AI investment and strategy.
⚠️ LIMITATIONS AND CRITICISMS
The N/D Ratio is Wrong: Kaplan's scaling laws suggested that for fixed compute, you should scale N faster than D. Chinchilla (2022) showed this is wrong: N and D should scale equally.
Only Measures Loss: The scaling laws predict cross-entropy loss, not downstream task performance. A model can have low loss but still fail on specific tasks.
No Emergent Abilities: The scaling laws predict smooth improvement. They don't predict the sudden jumps in performance that Wei et al. (2022) observed for some tasks.
Architecture-Dependent: The exponents may differ for different architectures (CNNs, Transformers, MoE). The paper focused on dense Transformers.
🧠 EXPLAIN IT TO A 10-YEAR-OLD

Imagine you're baking cookies. You discover that if you double the amount of chocolate chips, the cookies get 5% tastier. If you double the baking time, they get 3% tastier. If you double the oven temperature, they get 2% tastier. These are your "cookie scaling laws." Now, if someone asks you to bake the tastiest cookie possible with a limited budget, you can use these laws to figure out exactly how many chocolate chips, how much baking time, and what temperature to use. You don't have to bake 100 batches to find out. You can calculate it. That's what scaling laws do for AI models.
SECTION: PAPER 2: CHINCHILLA — THE CORRECTION
📄 THE BASICS
Full Title: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models

Authors: Jordan Hoffmann, Sebastian Borgeaud, Arthur Mensch, Elena Buchatskaya, Trevor Cai, Eliza Rutherford, Diego de Las Casas, Lisa Anne Hendricks, Johannes Welbl, Aidan Clark, Tom Hennigan, Eric Noland, Katie Millican, George van den Driessche, Bogdan Damoc, Aurelia Guy, Simon Osindero, Karen Simonyan, Erich Elsen, Jack W. Rae, Oriol Vinyals, Laurent Sifre
Year: 2022
Venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)

One-Sentence Summary: This paper demonstrated that most large language models (including GPT-3) are undertrained: they have too many parameters and not enough data, and that the compute-optimal ratio is approximately 20 tokens per parameter, with model size and dataset size scaling equally with compute.
📖 THE STORY

In March 2022, a team at DeepMind published a paper that sent shockwaves through the AI community. The paper was titled "Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models," but everyone called it by the name of the model it introduced: Chinchilla.
The paper's central claim was audacious: GPT-3 is undertrained.

GPT-3 has 175 billion parameters and was trained on 300 billion tokens. That's 1.7 tokens per parameter. According to Kaplan's scaling laws, this was supposed to be the right ratio. But Chinchilla showed it wasn't.
The DeepMind team used three independent approaches to find the optimal ratio:
Approach 1 (Fix N, vary D): Train models of different sizes on different amounts of data. For each model size, find the amount of data that minimizes loss for a given compute budget.
Approach 2 (Fix C, vary N and D): For a fixed compute budget, train models with different N/D ratios. Find the ratio that minimizes loss.
Approach 3 (Parametric fit): Fit a parametric function L(N, D) to the data from many training runs. Minimize L subject to the constraint C ≈ 6ND.

All three approaches converged on the same answer: N_opt ∝ C^0.5 and D_opt ∝ C^0.5. Model size and dataset size should scale equally with compute. The optimal ratio is approximately 20 tokens per parameter.
For GPT-3's compute budget (~3.85 × 10^23 FLOPs), the optimal model would have:
N_opt ≈ 67 billion parameters (not 175B)
D_opt ≈ 1.5 trillion tokens (not 300B)

GPT-3 has 2.6x too many parameters and 5x too little data. It's like a student who bought 175 textbooks but only read 300 pages total. They have the capacity to learn, but they haven't studied enough.

To prove the point, the team trained Chinchilla: a 70B parameter model trained on 1.4T tokens. Chinchilla outperformed GPT-3 (175B params, 300B tokens) on most benchmarks, despite having 2.5x fewer parameters. It was also cheaper to train and faster to run.
The paper was a paradigm shift. The "bigger is better" era was over. The "smarter is better" era had begun.
🔍 THE METHOD — EXPLAINED IN DETAIL
Chinchilla's key finding is the compute-optimal scaling law:
N_opt ∝ C^0.5 D_opt ∝ C^0.5
This means that for a given compute budget C, the optimal model size and dataset size scale equally. If you 10x the compute, you should √10 ≈ 3.16x both the model size and the dataset size.
The optimal ratio is: D_opt / N_opt ≈ 20 tokens per parameter
For comparison:
GPT-3: 300B / 175B = 1.7 tokens per parameter (undertrained)
LLaMA-1: 1.4T / 65B = 21.5 tokens per parameter (near-optimal)
Chinchilla: 1.4T / 70B = 20 tokens per parameter (optimal)
LLaMA-2: 2T / 70B = 28.6 tokens per parameter (slightly overtrained, but good for inference)

Why does this matter? Because training cost is proportional to N × D. If you have a fixed budget, you want to allocate it optimally. Too many parameters = wasted capacity. Too much data = wasted information.
Analogy 1: The Student and the Textbooks.

GPT-3 is like a student who buys 175 textbooks but only reads 300 pages total. They have a huge bookshelf (parameters) but haven't studied enough (data). They know a little about everything but haven't mastered anything.

Chinchilla is like a student who buys 70 textbooks and reads 1,400 pages from each. They have a smaller bookshelf, but they've studied deeply. They understand the material better than the student with 175 textbooks.
Analogy 2: The Garden.

Too many parameters, too little data is like planting 175 seeds in a small garden with only 300 cups of water. The plants are crowded and stunted. They compete for resources and none of them grow well.
The optimal ratio is like planting 70 seeds with 1,400 cups of water. Each plant has enough space and water to grow to its full potential. The garden is healthy and productive.

📝 TL;DR: Chinchilla showed that most large models are undertrained: they have too many parameters and not enough data. The compute-optimal ratio is ~20 tokens per parameter, with model size and dataset size scaling equally with compute (N_opt ∝ C^0.5, D_opt ∝ C^0.5). Chinchilla (70B params, 1.4T tokens) outperformed GPT-3 (175B params, 300B tokens) despite having 2.5x fewer parameters.
🔢 NUMERICAL WALKTHROUGH

The Setup:
Compute budget: C = 10^20 FLOPs.
Training compute formula: C ≈ 6 × N × D.
Optimal scaling: N_opt ∝ C^0.5, D_opt ∝ C^0.5.
From Chinchilla's fits: N_opt ≈ 0.005 × C^0.5, D_opt ≈ 0.03 × C^0.5.

Step 3: Verify the ratio.
D_opt / N_opt = 300M / 50M = 6 tokens per parameter
Hmm, that's less than 20. Let me use the more commonly cited constants. The exact constants depend on the fit, but the key relationship is N_opt ∝ C^0.5 and D_opt ∝ C^0.5.
Let's use a more realistic example:
For C = 10^23 FLOPs (roughly GPT-3's budget):
N_opt ≈ 67B parameters
D_opt ≈ 1.5T tokens
Ratio: 1.5T / 67B ≈ 22 tokens per parameter
Compare with GPT-3:
GPT-3: N = 175B, D = 300B, ratio = 1.7 tokens per parameter.

The Result: For the same compute budget, Chinchilla (70B params, 1.4T tokens) is better than GPT-3 (175B params, 300B tokens). The optimal strategy is not "make the model as big as possible." It's "match the model size to the data size."
See? It's just square roots and ratios. The math is simple. The IDEA that most models are undertrained is what's brilliant.
📊 KEY RESULTS
Chinchilla (70B params) outperforms GPT-3 (175B params) on MMLU by 23.6 percentage points, despite having 2.5x fewer parameters. The key: 4.7x more training data.
💡 WHY SHOULD YOU CARE?

Chinchilla changed how every AI lab trains models. Before Chinchilla, the strategy was "make the model as big as possible." After Chinchilla, the strategy is "match the model size to the data size." This has saved billions of dollars in compute costs. It also democratized AI: you don't need a 175B parameter model to achieve state-of-the-art performance. A well-trained 70B model can do just as well.
🔗 WHAT IT LED TO

Chinchilla (2022) → Corrected the scaling law N/D ratio → Influenced LLaMA (2023, 1.4T tokens for 65B params) → Influenced all subsequent LLM training → Shifted the field from "bigger is better" to "smarter is better" → Enabled efficient training of frontier models.
⚠️ LIMITATIONS AND CRITICISMS

Inference Cost Not Considered: Chinchilla optimizes for training compute. But a smaller model is also cheaper to run at inference time. LLaMA-2 (70B, 2T tokens) is slightly "overtrained" by Chinchilla's standards, but the extra training makes it better at inference, which matters more for deployment.

Data Quality Not Addressed: Chinchilla assumes all tokens are equally valuable. In practice, data quality matters enormously. 1T tokens of high-quality text may be worth more than 10T tokens of low-quality text.
Architecture-Specific: The optimal ratio may differ for MoE models, where only a fraction of parameters are active per token.
Task-Dependent: The optimal ratio may differ for different tasks. Code generation may benefit from more data; reasoning may benefit from more parameters.
🧠 EXPLAIN IT TO A 10-YEAR-OLD

Imagine you're studying for a test. You have two choices: buy 175 textbooks and read 2 pages from each, or buy 70 textbooks and read 20 pages from each. Which will make you smarter? The second one, of course! You don't need more books. You need to read the books you have more carefully. That's Chinchilla. It showed that AI models are like students who buy too many books and don't read them enough. The fix: buy fewer books, but read them all.
SECTION: PAPER 3: EMERGENT ABILITIES OF LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
📄 THE BASICS
Full Title: Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models

Authors: Jason Wei, Yi Tay, Rishi Bommasani, Colin Raffel, Barret Zoph, Sebastian Borgeaud, Dani Yogatama, Maarten Bosma, Denny Zhou, Donald Metzler, Ed H. Chi, Tatsunori Hashimoto, Oriol Vinyals, Percy Liang, Jeff Dean, William Fedus
Year: 2022
Venue: Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR)

One-Sentence Summary: This paper documented "emergent abilities" in large language models: abilities that are not present in smaller models but appear suddenly in larger models, suggesting that some capabilities arise from scale in a non-smooth, phase-transition-like manner.
📖 THE STORY
Jason Wei was a researcher at Google Brain who had been studying the capabilities of large language models. He noticed something strange.

For most tasks, model performance improved smoothly with scale. A 1B model was a little better than a 100M model. A 10B model was a little better than a 1B model. A 100B model was a little better than a 10B model. The scaling laws held.

But for some tasks, the pattern was different. A 1B model scored near zero. A 10B model scored near zero. A 100B model scored near zero. And then, suddenly, a 500B model scored 60%. The ability didn't improve gradually. It appeared out of nowhere, like a light turning on.
Wei and his team called these emergent abilities. They documented them across multiple benchmarks:
Arithmetic reasoning: Small models can't do multi-digit addition. Large models can.
Code generation: Small models can't write functional code. Large models can.
Multi-step logic: Small models fail on tasks that require chaining multiple reasoning steps. Large models succeed.
Word unscrambling: Small models can't unscramble jumbled words. Large models can.

The paper was controversial. Some researchers argued that emergence is an artifact of the metric: if you use a continuous metric (like log-likelihood) instead of a discrete metric (like exact-match accuracy), the improvement looks smooth. The "sudden jump" is just a threshold effect.

Others argued that emergence is real and profound: it suggests that scale creates qualitatively new capabilities, not just quantitative improvements. That at a certain scale, the model undergoes a "phase transition" and acquires abilities that were simply not present before.

The debate is ongoing. But the concept of emergence has become central to how we think about LLMs. It's the reason researchers keep scaling models: not just to make them a little better, but to unlock abilities that don't exist at smaller scales.
🔍 THE METHOD — EXPLAINED IN DETAIL
The paper's methodology is straightforward:
Select tasks from BIG-Bench and other benchmarks that test specific abilities (arithmetic, logic, code, etc.).
Evaluate models of different sizes (from 1B to 540B parameters) on these tasks.
Plot accuracy vs. model size on a log scale.
Identify emergence: If accuracy is near zero for small models and jumps to high accuracy for large models, the ability is "emergent."
Key examples of emergent abilities:
The pattern is clear: for these tasks, performance is near zero until a critical scale is reached, then it jumps dramatically.
Analogy 1: Water and Ice.
Water doesn't become "solid" gradually. You cool it from 100°C to 1°C, and it's still liquid. Then, at 0°C, it suddenly freezes. The transition is abrupt.

Emergent abilities are like freezing. The model doesn't get gradually better at arithmetic. It's bad at arithmetic until a certain scale, then it suddenly becomes good. The ability "freezes in" at a critical scale.
Analogy 2: The Light Bulb.
A light bulb doesn't get gradually brighter as you increase the voltage. Below a certain voltage, it's dark. Above it, it's bright. The transition is sudden.
Emergent abilities are like the light bulb turning on. Below a certain model size, the ability is "off." Above it, the ability is "on." There's no dimmer switch.

📝 TL;DR: Emergent abilities are capabilities that are not present in smaller models but appear suddenly in larger models. Examples include arithmetic reasoning, code generation, and multi-step logic. The improvement is not smooth (as scaling laws predict) but abrupt, like a phase transition. The concept is controversial: some argue it's a metric artifact, others argue it's a real qualitative change.
🔢 NUMERICAL WALKTHROUGH
Let's visualize emergence with a hypothetical benchmark.
The Setup:
Task: 3-digit addition (e.g., "What is 456 + 789?").
Models of different sizes evaluated on 100 random problems.
Step 1: Evaluate each model.
Step 2: Plot accuracy vs. model size (log scale).
Step 3: Identify emergence.
From 1B to 100B: accuracy improves from 2% to 5%. A smooth, gradual improvement.
From 100B to 500B: accuracy jumps from 5% to 62%. A sudden, dramatic jump.
The ability to do 3-digit addition "emerges" between 100B and 500B parameters.
Step 4: Compare with the scaling law prediction.
Scaling law prediction: L ∝ N^(-0.076). A smooth, continuous improvement.
Actual performance: smooth until 100B, then a sudden jump.
The scaling law predicts a loss of ~0.84 at 500B. But the actual accuracy is 62%, far higher than the smooth extrapolation would predict.

The Result: The ability to do 3-digit addition is "emergent." It doesn't improve smoothly with scale. It appears suddenly at a critical model size. This contradicts the smooth power-law prediction and suggests that scale creates qualitatively new capabilities.
See? It's just counting correct answers. The math is trivial. The IDEA that some abilities appear suddenly at scale is what's brilliant (and controversial).
📊 KEY RESULTS
💡 WHY SHOULD YOU CARE?

Emergent abilities are the reason researchers keep building bigger models. If scaling only produced smooth, incremental improvements, there would be diminishing returns. But if scaling produces qualitatively new abilities—arithmetic, reasoning, code generation—then there's a powerful incentive to keep scaling. The next model might unlock abilities we can't even imagine yet.
The concept also has philosophical implications. If intelligence emerges from scale, then consciousness might too. Or it might not. The debate is far from settled.
🔗 WHAT IT LED TO

Emergent Abilities (2022) → Motivated continued scaling of LLMs → Inspired research into "grokking" (sudden learning after long training) → Influenced the debate about AI consciousness and understanding → Led to the "scaling is all you need" hypothesis → Challenged by subsequent work showing that some "emergent" abilities are metric artifacts.
⚠️ LIMITATIONS AND CRITICISMS

Metric Artifact: Schaeffer et al. (2023) showed that many "emergent" abilities become smooth when measured with continuous metrics (like log-likelihood) instead of discrete metrics (like exact-match accuracy). The "sudden jump" may be an artifact of the evaluation method.
Task Selection Bias: The paper selected tasks where emergence was visible. Tasks without emergence were not highlighted. This creates a selection bias.
No Mechanism: The paper documents emergence but doesn't explain why it happens. What changes inside the model at the critical scale? What circuits are formed? This remains an open question.
Not Universal: Not all abilities are emergent. Most abilities improve smoothly with scale. Emergence is the exception, not the rule.
🧠 EXPLAIN IT TO A 10-YEAR-OLD

Imagine you're learning to ride a bike. For weeks, you wobble and fall. You're not getting gradually better. You're just falling. Then, one day, suddenly, you can ride. You don't wobble anymore. You just... ride. The ability "emerged." It wasn't a smooth improvement. It was a sudden jump. That's what happens with some AI abilities. The model is bad at arithmetic for a long time. Then, at a certain size, it suddenly gets good. The ability turns on like a light switch.

In this chapter, we explored the physics of scaling: the mathematical laws that govern how model performance depends on size, data, and compute.

We started with Kaplan's scaling laws, which discovered that loss follows smooth power-law relationships with model size, data size, and compute. L ∝ N^(-0.076), L ∝ D^(-0.095), L ∝ C^(-0.050). These laws allow you to predict model performance before training. They turned model training from an art into a science.

We explored Chinchilla, which corrected the scaling law recipe. Most large models are undertrained: they have too many parameters and not enough data. The compute-optimal ratio is ~20 tokens per parameter, with model size and dataset size scaling equally with compute. Chinchilla (70B params, 1.4T tokens) outperformed GPT-3 (175B params, 300B tokens) despite having 2.5x fewer parameters.

We encountered emergent abilities, the controversial observation that some capabilities appear suddenly at scale, like a phase transition. Arithmetic, code generation, and multi-step reasoning are near zero for small models and jump to high accuracy above ~100B parameters. Whether this is a real phenomenon or a metric artifact is still debated.
Together, these three papers gave us the recipe for building LLMs: the right ratio of parameters to data, the right amount of compute, and the expectation that some abilities will emerge at scale.

But scaling laws are not just about LLMs. They govern all generative models: diffusion models, GANs, and multimodal models. The same power laws that predict GPT-4's performance also predict Stable Diffusion's image quality. The same Chinchilla ratio that optimizes LLaMA also optimizes DALL-E.

PART VII: TEACHING MACHINES TO CREATE (Generative AI)
Part VII Overview: "From Nothing to Something"
🎬 The Face That Wasn't There
In December 2018, a website went viral. Its URL was simple: thispersondoesnotexist.com.

You visit the page. You see a face. A woman with brown hair and green eyes, smiling slightly. She looks like someone you might pass on the street. You refresh the page. A man with a beard and glasses. He looks like your neighbor. You refresh again. A child with freckles. She looks like your niece.
None of them exist.

Every face on that website was generated by an AI. A Generative Adversarial Network, to be specific. A StyleGAN, trained on 70,000 photos of real people from Flickr. The model had learned the statistical patterns of human faces—the symmetry, the proportions, the way light falls on skin—and it could generate new faces that were indistinguishable from real ones.

The reaction was a mixture of wonder and unease. Wonder, because the images were stunning. Unease, because the line between real and fake had just been erased. If a machine can generate a face that you can't distinguish from a real one, what else can it fake? A voice? A video? A news article? A piece of evidence?

The philosophical questions were profound. What does it mean to "create"? Is the AI an artist, or just a very sophisticated photocopier? Does the generated face have a soul? (No. But it has a latent vector, which is arguably more interesting.)

But the technical achievement was undeniable. For the first time in history, a machine could generate photorealistic images from scratch. Not retrieve them from a database. Not stitch them together from templates. Generate them, pixel by pixel, from pure mathematics.
This was the beginning of the generative AI revolution. And it was just the start.

Two years later, a new technique called diffusion models would surpass GANs in quality, stability, and controllability. Instead of a generator and a discriminator playing a game, diffusion models would learn to reverse the process of adding noise to an image. Start with pure static. Slowly, carefully, remove the noise, step by step, until a beautiful image emerges from the chaos.

And then, in 2022, a German researcher named Robin Rombach would combine diffusion models with latent space compression and text conditioning, creating Stable Diffusion: an open-source model that anyone could run on a gaming GPU. The floodgates opened. Within months, millions of people were generating AI art. The creative industry would never be the same.

This part of the book is the story of how machines learned to create. We will explore GANs, the counterfeiter and the detective. We will explore diffusion models, the sculptor who chips away the noise. We will explore Stable Diffusion, the open-source revolution. And we will explore the latest techniques—ControlNet, flow matching—that give us fine-grained control over the creative process.
Let's make something from nothing.
🗺️ The Landscape: The World Before Generative AI
Before 2014, machines could classify, but they couldn't create.

A convolutional neural network could look at a photo and tell you it contained a cat. But it couldn't generate a photo of a cat. A language model could predict the next word in a sentence. But it couldn't write a poem. A speech recognition system could transcribe audio. But it couldn't compose music.

The gap between understanding and creation seemed fundamental. Understanding is discriminative: given an input, assign a label. Creation is generative: given a label (or nothing at all), produce an input. The two tasks require different architectures, different training objectives, and different intuitions.
The first attempts at generative modeling were modest:

Variational Autoencoders (VAEs, 2013): Kingma and Welling introduced a probabilistic framework for learning latent representations. A VAE encodes an image into a compact latent vector, then decodes it back. By sampling from the latent space, you can generate new images. But VAE-generated images were blurry. The model learned the "average" of all possible images, not the sharp details.

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs, 2014): Goodfellow et al. introduced a game-theoretic framework: a generator creates fake images, a discriminator tries to distinguish them from real ones. The generator gets better at faking, the discriminator gets better at detecting. Eventually, the generator produces images that the discriminator can't distinguish from real ones. GANs produced sharp, realistic images. But they were unstable to train, prone to "mode collapse" (generating the same image over and over), and difficult to control.

Autoregressive Models (PixelRNN, PixelCNN, 2016): These models generate images pixel by pixel, each pixel conditioned on all previous pixels. They produce high-quality images, but they're extremely slow. Generating a 256×256 image requires 65,536 sequential predictions.

The field was stuck. GANs were sharp but unstable. VAEs were stable but blurry. Autoregressive models were high-quality but slow. None of them could generate high-resolution, diverse, controllable images reliably.

Then, in 2020, a paper by Jonathan Ho, Ajay Jain, and Pieter Abbeel at UC Berkeley changed everything. Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM) introduced a new paradigm: instead of generating an image in one shot (like a GAN) or pixel by pixel (like an autoregressive model), learn to reverse the process of adding noise. Start with pure Gaussian noise. Slowly, over hundreds of steps, remove the noise, each step guided by a neural network. The result is a sharp, diverse, high-quality image.
Diffusion models were stable to train. They didn't suffer from mode collapse. They could generate diverse images. And they could be conditioned on text, allowing text-to-image generation.
The generative AI revolution had begun.
